performance.p: First Performed at the Royal Olympic Theatre, (under the management of Mr. Horace Wigan) on Saturday, March 4th, 1865, a New and Original Play, in Five Acts, by Tom Taylor Esq., called
SETTLING DAY, A STORY OF THE TIME.
The New Scenery by Mr. HAWES CRAVEN. The Dresses by Mr. S. MAY and Mrs. LEWIS.
The Properties by Mr. LIGHTFOOT. The Machinery by Mr. CHAPMAN.
The whole Produced under the Direction of Mr. HORACE WIGAN.

list.item: Act 1.—AT HOME. Scene—MORNING ROOM IN MARKLAND’S VILLA ON THE THAMES.
Act 2.—IN THE CITY. Scene—Stockbroker's Office, with View of Capel Court & Entrance of the Stock Exchange.
Act 3.—BEHIND THE SCENES. Scene—A WEST-END BANK PARLOUR.
Act 4.—THE BIRTHDAY FETE. Scene—Reception Room in Markland’s Villa.
Act 5.—THE RIVER TERRACE. Scene—The Grounds of Markland’s Villa, with the River and DISTANT VIEW OF LONDON, BY MOONLIGHT.

div.head: Act I. At Hpme.
div.stage: SCENE.—A drawing-room in Markland's Villa, Putney, luxuriously and elegantly furnished. Communicating with it c, at back, a spacious conservatory ornamented with statuary and filled with exotics in the most gorgeous beauty of foliage and flower. Doors R. and L. range of French windows R., commanding view of grounds and the river; fire-place R. 3. E., under c. window.
Glover—a footman—and Cresswell discovered as in eager conversation, he remonstrating, she insisting.

sp.speaker: Glover.
sp.p: Well, but I can't tell one gent missus is at home and another she ain't.

sp.speaker: Cress.
sp.p: It ain't our business, Glover, to make messages fit; them's my orders.

sp.speaker: Glover.
sp.p: (looking out of window r.) Well, but there's Mr. Meiklam got off already. There's one o' the gardener's boys holding his mare, and a nice looking tit she is.

sp.speaker: Cress.
sp.p: Just like his impudence—Mr. Harrington ain't half as free, and he's twice as welcome.

sp.speaker: Frank Meiklam.
sp.p: (heard outside R. U. E.) Walk her about quietly, my lad.

div.stage: Enter Frank, from window R.U. E.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Oh, Mrs. Markland's maid, I think. (Cresswell curtsies)(to Footman) You took in my card ?

sp.speaker: Glover.
sp.p: Yes, sir. (aside to Cresswell) You'd better do it. (exit L. 3 E.)

sp.speaker: Cress.
sp.p: (hastily) Mrs. Markland's compliments, sir, and she's sorry she's particularly engaged.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (sits R.) Oh, very well, en attendant—Miss Hargreave will do.

sp.speaker: Cress.
sp.p: (aside) Do, indeed ! I should think she would. Well, he've come in hisself. I'll ask in the other.

div.stage: (exit R.U.E.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (writing at table R., and speaking as he writes) Say if Miss Hargreave will give me five minutes—(looks up) Eh! the girl's gone—cool, but these ladies' maids are about the coolest lot—

div.stage: Re-enter Cresswell, showing in Harrington, R.U.E.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (rising and taking stage l.) How do, Harrington ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (stiffly, coming down R.) Good morning.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (to Cresswell) Say if Miss Hargreave will give me five minutes—

sp.speaker: Cress.
sp.p: Miss Hargreave's compliments, sir, and she's particularly engaged too.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: You know that's a crammer, you little—(coming up to her insolently.)

sp.speaker: Cress.
sp.p: Sir! (indignantly) Well, I'm sure ! (he puts his hand to his pocket) No, sir, I'll trouble you to keep yourself to yourself and your money too.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Oh, very well, Mrs. Captain Grand. Here, take this to your mistress, and say I'm in the drawing­room (gives her envelope with opera-box ticket, on which he has been writing). Deuced overbearing that style of young woman!

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Yes, they can generally give as good as they get.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (looking out of window r.) Nice horse that in your brougham. I like your turn out, it's so quiet.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Ah, I prefer things quiet, (pause.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Elegant house Markland's got here, (no answer) Capital style about everything in the place.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (aside) Except one of the visitors.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Waiting for Markland ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: I thought you might be; he used to have no end of fellows always waiting for him before his marriage ; since then he has been so awfully spoony on his wife he seems to have cut the shop altogether.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: The shop ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: The bank, I mean. Well, I don't wonder: both Mrs. Markland and her sister are girls to knock a fellow over—rather. I've just sent them in a bone for the opera. Miss Hargreave's wild about " Faust" and Patti. (lounges on couch L.) Go much to the opera ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: I've a stall for the Thursdays and Saturdays.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Ah, not for Tuesdays ? Sorry I can't offer you a place, but four's one too many.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: I quite agree with you. (strolls up—aside) Snob !

div.stage: Re-enter Cresswell, L. U, E., with envelope.

sp.speaker: Cress.
sp.p: Missus's compliments, (maliciously) she's sorry she's engaged for Tuesday, (returning envelope to Frank.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (annoyed) Oh!

sp.speaker: Cress.
sp.p: And she's particularly sorry she can't have the pleasure of seeing you this morning, (to Harrington) I was to say, sir, if you would have the plant you've brought put into the conservatory missus will see you as soon as she can.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Upon my word that's coolish—(tearing up envelope) isn't it ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Perhaps Mrs. Markland agrees with you that four's one too many.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (going up) Ah, very good, (stopping and speaking out of window R., angrily) What do you mean by letting my mare stand still, you blockhead ? (going up for hat) Good morning, (to Harrington.)

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (drily) Good morning, (at window R.) Take that gardenia out of my brougham carefully—thank you.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (coming down with hat) Oh, that's your plant, is it?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (out of window R.) Gently, my man. Yes, I brought it for Mrs. Markland, she wanted one for her fête to-night.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (aside) So, a fête to-night and I'm not asked, (to Harrington) Ah, yes; shall you be here ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Yes—shall you ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: I hardly know. I've so many engagements. (aside) Stuck up beggar! (putting on his gloves angrily) Well, he's on the right side of the ropes this morning. (pausing) I wonder if Belle—no, it's all her sister's doing. If I don't make her pay for this yet.

div.stage: (Two Footmen enter R. 2 E., carrying gardenia—they go towards conservatory c.)
Enter Miss Hargreave, D. L. U. E.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: (meeting Servants) The new gardenia—oh, stop, Glover, do stop, and let me look at it. What a lovely plant!

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (going up) And it's as sweet as it's beautiful, Miss Hargreave.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Harrington, Florry will be so delighted—not Mr. Markland, though—he was talking of driving to Veitch's to secure this new beauty; he had set his heart on having it at Florry's party to-night. You know it's her birthday.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Yes, a bride's birthday should be marked with flowers.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Especially so happy a bride as Florry : only two-and-twenty, and the world lying before her in the triple sunshine of youth, love, and prosperity ! May she have many birthdays as bright as this.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Why, Miss Hargreave, you talk like a matron instead of a young lady of nineteen.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p:
Nineteen ! why I was one-and-twenty last
month, but nobody thought of marking my birthday with flowers.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: I wish I had known of it.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: An old woman may be excused for keeping these anniversaries in the background.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: An old woman ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Yes, I'm my own mistress now, and I feel so grave and steady.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Why one would fancy you were the chaperone, and Mrs. Markland under your wing.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Oh, Florry's not half such a woman of busi­ness as I am. I understand accounts and trusts and separate uses. I even think I could draw my own dividends.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Now you're joking—I hope you're joking.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Joking ? Is a woman who can draw her own dividends such an appalling phenomenon ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Well, you see I've a notion, somehow, a woman has no business to know anything about money —except how to spend it, of course.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I hope, when you marry, your wife won't make you change your theory.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: My wife! Ah, Miss Hargreave, if I only durst—I've caught the honeymoon fever in this house— the sight of Markland's happiness is enough to make any bachelor throw himself right——

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Into the Thames ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: No, into matrimony; seriously, Miss Hargreave, can you conceive a happier man than your brother-in-law—born to wealth, respect out of doors, and affection within, the present all sunshine, the future all promise ! What has he done to deserve it ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: He had the good luck to be born heir to an old established bank business, and the good taste to fall in love with my sister.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Oh, Miss Hargreave, if I could follow his example!

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: What, you fall in love with Florry, too ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p:
No, but with ——(Mr. and Mrs.
Markland heard outside in the conservatory, c, in playful contest.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I tell you, Florry, I daren't keep them waiting any longer, (they appear in conservatory, he dragged along by her.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Then I dare, and I'm absolute to-day ! You're my prisoner, (holding his hands in hers, and down, R. c.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Look here, Harrington, this is what you'll come to some day.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: I hope so, heartily. I'm quite ready. (Holding out his hands to Miss Hargreave) Miss Hargreave, will you put on the handcuffs ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Harrington, if you knew the trouble I've had to secure this truant. I've caught him flying, between a directorate and a deputation, and dragged him here in triumph to see the beautiful gardenia you've brought me.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: It's too bad, Harrington, forestalling one in this way.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Serves you right, sir, for forgetting your wife's birthday presents to attend to your business.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Why, you unreasonable little woman, I haven't given a day to the bank since we were married.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: No, but you're going to ; and what right have you to make appointments here, where your only business ought to be spoiling me ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I appeal to you, Harrington, if I haven't done that piece of business handsomely. I've been six months about it, but I've done it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: No, no, no; if ever there was an ill-used wife I am one.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Prove it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: In the first place, I'm never contradicted—I appeal to Belle, if he don't let me have my own way in everything.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: He's incorrigible.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I plead guilty, but I'll never do it again.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: And then I'm not allowed to have any little whims and fancies; am I, Belle ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: No ; your husband in the most cruel way insists on anticipating them all.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I'll say no to everything you propose for the next month.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But worse than all, I've a rival.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: A rival!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: The deuce you have !

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, an old love. Her initials are L. S. D. I thought the connection was broken off, but he's going back to her. He'll spend more of his time on L. S. D. now than he does on poor P. M.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (R.) Ah, Florry, business is a hard master. I never knew how hard till I left him for love, and the delicious dream of the last half year——

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Dream ! he calls our married life a dream—I said I was cruelly treated.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And could anything but a dream be so delightful ? (this should be spoken in a tone of dreamy but enthusiastic reminiscence, warming into tenderness as the speech proceeds.) Among the wonders of the Alps, to feel the savage sublimity of nature heightened by the sense of love and trust, as I turned from peak and glacier to the wife who nestled at my side! Under the cloudless Italian sky, to visit the marvels of art in the famous cities of the past, and feel their desolation the more keenly for its contrast with the young life that was given to my charge, the pure joy reflected in the face that looked up to mine ! But all that is over now.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (tenderly nestling to his side) The dream, perhaps, but not the double life and the reflected joy.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: They will shine all the brighter for a sombre background of business. But I promise to lock up L. S. D. in the bank parlour. Let's hope she won't get through the keyhole.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Amen ! But do you know, Harry, I sometimes have such a wicked wish.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, I sometimes wish that we could be ——

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Be what ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Just a little ruined!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (startled) Ruined! don't talk nonsense, Florry.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Because then I fancy I might show you the real good of a wife. As it is I seem little better than a spoiled child to be dressed up and made much of. I'm no earthly use—what can I do ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Be happy, my darling, and make me happy in that happiness. Bring that bright and trustful face to welcome me when I return worn and weary from my day's work at the gold diggings. If you only knew what strength, what comfort I shall find in it. But don't pray for ruin even in jest, (very earnestly)

div.stage: Enter Footman with card, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Molesworth!

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (rising) My guardian! Miss Hargreave, I wish you'd show me your aviary, I'm so fond of small birds.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: And I'm a great bird-tamer—my prisoners are so fond of me.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: I should think so. (they go up c.)

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: You'll find us in the conservatory, Florry.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (looking at card, reads) "Two words on business." Mayn't I ? (playfully to his wife.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Let me see—well, yes; prisoner may be allowed to see his attorney. (exit Servant l. d.) (going up c.) I must find a place for this beautiful plant. (to Markland) Mind, only "two words "—and remember —" the warder has her eye on you." (kisses him and exit c.)

div.stage: Enter Molesworth, L. 3 E.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Excuse my breaking in on you here, but the fact is I'm kept so busy with other people's affairs I find it difficult to get a moment for my own.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p:
Pretty much my case, now I'm going back into harness. I've a deputation waiting for me in the break­fast room. It's about the vacant seat for Cashiobury. They insist on having a monied man, and flatter
themselves I'm ready to drop £2,000 for the honour of writing myself M.P.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Don't have anything to say to them. I can get it done for you at half the money. Egad ! I'm just in time it seems, (takes letter from his pocket) Here's old Hookham, that we've been agent for since the time of legal memory, writes to me from Closeborough begging me to offer you the seat as "a man of the right sort."

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Does that mean Whig or Tory ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Oh, the constituency is not particular about the colour of your ribbons, so that it sees the colour of your money. It's the snuggest, quietest, most eligible thing, in a small way, in the Parliamentary market; constituency under four hundred, and only fifty stand out for cash. Hookham's got the seat in his pocket— say the word, I'll send you down, and he'll return you, like a good bill, duly stamped and lettered M.P.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You're very kind. This is the third borough I've had offered me this week; I hear people talk about the difficulty of getting a seat—my difficulty's to keep out of one.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Ah, you're the sort of man a British constituency fastens on.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes, your deputation leech especially. Translated into their tongue, a man of the right sort, means a man who will spend money. They've a stupid notion all bankers are rich.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: As if all were gold that glitters, (laughing) But all this is your business—I want to speak to you about my own. You know Harrington has just come of age ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I've received £40,000 of his money—the proceeds of a paid-off mortgage. I want to have it ready for him. I thought of leaving it with you for the present at call.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You must ask Meiklam. I've been a sleeping partner for the last six months. I should think we've quite as much in our hands as we know what to do with in the present state of the market. Hadn't you better buy exchequer bills or consols ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: What! in the face of the heavy fall ? I'd rather leave the money in your hands till I pay it over, so if you'll give me a lift as far as Lincoln's Inn; I must look in there, and you can take me to the bank at once.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Markland, C.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: But this deputation—I ought to see them.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Throw them over. Closeborough's decidedly a better investment—only half the price, and the seat's as safe as your own bank.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (laughs) I'll give these Cashiobnry fellows their congé at once, and knock off an address to the free and independent electors of Closeborough for you to send to Hookham—five minutes will do it. (going R.) But mind, not a word to my wife about the new seat, (exit R. 1.E.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (comes down on l. of Molesworth, shaking her finger playfully in his face) Oh, you wicked elderly man, conspiring with my prisoner !

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I'm an attorney—all my communications are privileged.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: You ! a married man, with a grey head and a grown up family, to tempt my husband with a seat in parliament, and before we've been six months married!

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I admit it's not fair to the constituency.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Not fair to the constituency ! Is it fair to his wife, sir ? Now he's come back to work, business will rob me of him all day, and you would have politics take him from me all night! Every British wife who loves her husband is bound to hate the House of Commons.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: For the first six months of matrimony : after that, a good many come to agree with their husbands, that the House is the most agreeable club in London.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p:
Yes, that's what comes of late hours, unlimited command of latch-keys, and male gossip in the smoking­room. Oh, I've studied the constitution of my country—I know what goes on inside Mr. Barry's pie-crust. They pretend to make laws, but they're really laying their heads together against their poor unoffending wives. I say the House of Commons will be a bane to society, until
yon make a large gallery for the ladies, and prevent every husband from opening his lips, till he catches his wife's eye as well as the speaker's. Oh, what capital whippers in we should make !

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: And what a pleasant berth the prime minister's would be, trying to keep his supporters' wives in good humour, instead of their lords and masters.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Now remember, if you dare, to aid and abet my husband in getting into parliament I shall let down my back hair, go distracted, and haunt Lincoln's Inn Fields in a black bombazine and a poke bonnet to lay my broken heart every morning at your door.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: They say a good many attorneys' doors are paved with that sort of thing already ; but I'm a family solicitor; we don't break hearts in our branch of the profession—but I musn't keep your husband waiting.

div.stage: (exit R. 1. E.)
Enter Footman with card, which he gives to Mrs. Markland.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Mrs. Vernon !

sp.speaker: Footman.
sp.p: She asked if you were at home, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: What a bore ! I suppose I must see her—say I'm at home, (exit Servant l.) She wished to catch Harry for her own daughter, but he had too much taste, and now she insists on petting me—but I don't like being petted, except by some people. She purrs over me so sweetly, I can't help expecting that some day she'll turn round and scratch.

div.stage: Enter Servant, L. 3 E.

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.p: (announcing) Mrs. Vernon.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Vernon, D. L. 3. E.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: I never saw your conservatory in such beauty. (coming down) Nor you either, you darling, (embracing her) You certainly are the prettiest mistress of the prettiest house!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I'm so glad you admire it. (they sit.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: (L. c) And all, thanks to your perfect taste. Mr. Markland has the good sense to leave the reins in your hands, I see—the husband to make the money, the wife to spend it: that's exactly my notion of the division of labour! And how lovely you are looking! You mustn't mind an old woman saying what she thinks. And so you are still very happy, eh ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (r. c.) I should be the most ungrateful woman, if I wasn't. Oh, Mrs Vernon, if you knew how good he is, how tender, how thoughtful.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: And you haven't felt the change from honey lunacy to the sober realities of married life too great a contrast ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, there has been no change as yet.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Then it will be all the worse when it does come. I suppose he's returned to work now ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, and I'm so sorry.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Ah, my dear, trust an old woman, one who has seen something of the world. Thank your stars you've married a man of business.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: What, to be separated from him all day long, and to know that when he's away his head is full—not of me—but of horrid money matters !

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Keeps him out of mischief, my dear. Men will be men! Wives are all very well, but they mustn't expect to fill up all a man's thoughts. Besides, he can't afford to neglect business: the bank must be looked after —with their enormous transactions there's a constant risk.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But you don't suppose my husband has any cause for anxiety ? I should be wretched if I thought so : as it is, I often wish he would give up the bank.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: What would become of his pretty house, his pretty grounds, and his pretty wife, and her pretty dresses, and carriages, and horses if he did ? Instead of wishing him to give up money, making you ought to learn to like it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, I never could do that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p:
I thought as you do once, but I've changed
my mind now. Why, my dear, the first thing I look at in the Times is the City Article, and the drive I most enjoy is to my broker's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, Mrs. Vernon, now you're joking with me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Fact, I assure you. A woman at my time of life must have an object. I've been disappointed in my hopes of settling my poor child : I don't care for books; I've no turn for religion, so I've taken to speculation; you can't think how amusing it is.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But isn't it wrong for a woman to know anything about such matters ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: So the men say: they want to keep the money-making to themselves, like their clubs and cigars, and Greenwich dinners.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I always fancied the city the dullest place, and money-making the dreariest drudgery.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Dull ? Dreary ? You little goose ! 'Tis life in its very essence—all the excitement of passion without its punishment, and all the delight of gambling stripped of its disreputableness. (rising) I've a great mind to carry you off in my brougham to my broker's this morning, and give you an insight into the sort of thing your husband will have to spend his life amongst.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (rising) Oh, what fun! To surprise Harry with my city experiences—and then I should like to astonish Belle, too—she gives herself such airs on the strength of her knowledge of business. It would sound so imposing, (with mock importance) "When I was with Mrs. Vernon, at her broker's."

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: No, no, my love, that would never do; very great ladies and very proper ladies go into the city, but they never tell. Not a word to your husband or your sister, or anybody else, promise me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Of course I will! There, solemnly!

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: I've a call or two to make ; get your things on and I'll be back for you by the time you're ready.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p:
I shan't be ten minutes; it will be such an adventure, and I promised to pick Harry up at the bank
this afternoon, (with mirthful mystery) There's a birth­day present in petto, but I'm supposed to know nothing abont it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: You sly little puss ! Au revoir then. Kindest regards to your husband. (Mrs. Markland rings bell, R. Aside) No clouds yet! They really do seem happy. Well, we shall see how long it will last, (turns, and very gushingly) Good-bye, you dear ! (exit, L. 3 E.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: After all Harry must be right: she does seem very fond of me: I was wrong to distrust her.

div.stage: Enter Markland and Molesworth, R. 1 E.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Now, Florry, kiss me, and call me a good boy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Not till I know why.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I've thrown over the Cashiobury deputation, the very thing you asked me to do.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Because I asked you ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Oh, you unbelieving woman ! What but your wish would have induced me to refuse the offer of a safe seat ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: The offer of a safer seat, at half the money. Ah, didn't I say the warder had her eye on you, and her ear too ? But it's no use. I've opened Mr. Molesworth's eyes to his own guilt. He'll look out for another victim, won't you, Mr. Molesworth ? Now there's your ward, Mr. Harrington.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Pooh, he's too young. Then he hasn't that sheet anchor of the British legislator—a wife.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But he soon will have, if I've eyes in my head. Oh, Harry, I'm so happy, do you know—but no, it's Belle's secret. Do go and offer Harrington the seat, Mr. Molesworth, you'll find him in the conservatory.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (crustily) Oh, he's here, is he ? Silly fellow !

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Silly fellow ! What, for calling on us ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: No, that's sensible, but I'm very angry with him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Angry.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: He's been dabbling on the Stock Exchange, and what's worse he's burnt his fingers severely.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Let him thank his stars for that.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: What, for losing several hundred pounds ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Better lose seven thousand in his first venture, than win ten times the money. Losing may disgust and deter, but winning is honey on the edge of the poisoned cup. The sweetness once tasted, let who will warn against the bitterness, the death that lies at the bottom. (passionately) Ah, Molesworth, if you love Harrington, thank heaven in your prayers to-night that his first venture has been a losing one.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (coming c.) Ah, how I wish all young men had such a counsellor, Mr. Molesworth.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Ah, it's easy lo advise.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But your advice is backed up by practice.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (to Molesworth) She's the most unblushing flatterer——

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: And pray who sets me the example, sir ? (to Molesworth) But I won't have any quarrel on my birthday that I can make up, so come, let me reconcile you and Harrington.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Oh, the foolish lad knows my way.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, that you're the most dreadful bear. If you had seen his alarm when you were announced. I left him in the conservatory with Belle. We'll pounce on him, the old bear and the young—what ? (playfully to Markland.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Monkey!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (ruefully) Oh, Harry, if you must go to the Zoological Gardens for a comparison, do find a prettier one. Come, Mr. Molesworth, now ain't I an ill-used wife ?

div.stage: (exeunt Molesworth and Mrs. Markland, C.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Bless her bright face, it is something worth living for to feel and minister to such happiness.

div.stage: Enter Footman, D. L. 3. E.

sp.speaker: Footman.
sp.p: A gent, sir, won't give his name, says he comes by appointment.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (looking at his watch) Appointment! I made no appointment after eleven.

div.stage: Enter Rocket, L. D. 3 E.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Oh, dear yes, you did. My name is Rocket; I'm an old friend of your partner's; this is the first time I've had the pleasure of seeing you, but we are no strangers.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I really don't remember ———

sp.speaker: Rock.
sp.p: (interrupting') Not remember ? Oh dear me, yes, you do ; just run your mind over the most brilliant ideas, financial, engineering, social or speculative, that have come under your eye lately in the shape of prospectuses —mostly provisional.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Oh, I remember now, Mr. Rocket, the companies' promoter, one of those daring pioneers on the frontiers of speculation, who go out with a project for their pick, and the wide world of noodledom for their gold diggings.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Ha, ha! (laughing good humouredly) I knew we knew each other; money and mind are bound to know each other in these go-ahead times. Mind, as I often say to my directors, mind is the steam, money is the locomotive. Without steam what's the engine ? Inert iron. Without the engine what is steam ? Vapour in vacuo; but bring 'em together, and what are they—the force that re-moulds the world!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And occasionally bursts its boilers in the process.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Yes, accidents will happen, but we ought to congratulate ourselves, my dear sir—

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: On escaping the smash ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Or having lived to see the triumph of the miracle-working power of co-operative capital.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes, associated capital is a great force, though some of you projectors seem to think that, in fact, as on paper, hundreds may be turned into millions merely by the addition of noughts.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Ha, ha, it's the order of nature. What ia mankind but a joint stock company of mites —

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (interrupting) Limited by time and space. But I think you said you came by appointment.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Yes, my own appointment,—by letter, yester­day afternoon. I sent a commissionaire with it to the bank—you didn't get it ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (dryly) No!

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Then it must have been late, or perhaps, the fellow didn't deliver it. I must send to the barracks to inquire. These irregularities, if repeated, will be fatal to the corps. By the way, I was the first to suggest a company for the employment of our wounded soldiers,— unluckily that was before we had any wounded soldiers to employ. Then came the war and the wounded soldiers, and, as usual, somebody else snapped up my idea. It's been my fate to be robbed of my ideas. The perambulator, sir, was my idea, but while I was organising a great international perambulator company, an outsider stepped in with an inferior article and run me off the road. Ah, sir, I ought to have gone down to posterity in my own perambulator, and children yet unborn should have blessed my name. However, as I was saying, I made an appointment with you. Here I am and here you are, and now my dear sir, (pointing to chair) "a nous deux," as the French say !

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (ringing bell, R.) Excuse me, Mr. Rocket "a vous seul," as the French say. I've a particular engagement and as this appointment is of your own making you will the more easily understand my declining it.

div.stage: Enter Footman, L. 3.E.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (seated l. c.) One moment! (to Servant) Never mind, my man, it was to open the door for me, but I'll let myself out. (to Markland) Send him away; we can't talk confidentially with a third party in the room.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Well, this is the coolest hand ! (motions to Servant, who exits l. 3. E.) Now, sir, as we are relieved of the presence of a third party, will you allow me to tell you that this is a gross intrusion of yours ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p:
I know it, my dear sir, I blush for it, but I must do it. I've a mission—a sacred mission to bring together mind and money. If mind is forced to intrude
itself upon money, so much the worse for mind. If money loses its temper with mind, so much the worse for money.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (standing R.) And if money takes the liberty of showing mind the door, and mind won't take the hint—

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (interrupting) Money is sure to repent of being hasty! I won't detain you ten minutes, (persuasively to Markland) We are both men of business. I have several fortunes to offer, (taking out prospectuses) and I've come to give you the choice of them. Here are six of my Directorates—provisional—competing for the honour of offering you a chair, (points to chair, R.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Mr. Rocket, do you take me for what in City slang is called a guinea-pig, one of those easy-going gentlemen who sell their names for a director's fee and a director's patronage?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Quite the reverse, my dear sir,—now don't be hasty, (motions Markland to take chair—he sits R. c.) Here's a magnificent thing—"the Metropolitan Cold Water Heating and Oxygenated Respiration Company." Let me develope the idea. Of course, you're aware of the apprehension entertained by scientific men of the approaching exhaustion of our coal fields or carbonaceous strata. You are no doubt familiar with the chemical composition of water—one part of hydrogen to eight of oxygen—the former, one of the most inflammable heating bodies in nature, the latter the great life-giving element of the air we breathe. I start from two great data—the importance of dispensing with coal, and the value of pure air to the animal economy. My scheme is to decompose the water of our noble metropolitan river by powerful voltaic action—to employ the oxygen thus set free for the vitalizing of the London atmosphere, and to convert the hydrogen to the unpretending, but highly important, purposes of house warning.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Literally setting the Thames on fire ? But how's London to manage without the river ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p:
Ah, there comes in my supplementary scheme —"The Grand Thames Valley Surface Drainage
Company," for creating a new Thames, of twice the volume and ten times the purity, of its predecessor. Stupendous idea, isn't it ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (dryly) Colossal! but I think I can improve upon it. Suppose after London has breathed all the oxygen and burnt all the hydrogen in the river, we were to collect the results, and start another company to recompose poor old Father Thames on the spot.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Ecod, there's something in that ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: It would be only keeping the old boy out of his bed for a week or two—and we might have it made, in interval. But seriously, Mr. Rocket, you seem to forget that I am a banker; my business is safe investment not rash adventure—I have a horror of speculation.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: My dear sir, don't disclaim one of the finest attributes of our nature!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: No, if I did take to blowing bubbles, they should be soap, not speculation ones. Allow me to wish you a good morning.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: You abuse speculation—when your house has been backing up the Great Rocky-mountain Trunk line so heavily ? You have backed it, haven't you ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Really, Mr. Rocket, I'm not aware our house owes you an account of its investments.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Oh, I merely repeat what's whispered in the City.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: The persons who repeat such whispers are as bad as those who originate them.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Why, you see Rocky-mountain Trunks are at a discount; and in these cases people will ask who's likely to be hard hit.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (angrily) Do you think, because I've listened patiently to your fantastic schemes, that I will sit patiently to hear the credit of our house blown upon, even by so loose a tongue as yours, sir ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: I withdraw my observation. But I certainly fancied from what I heard in Warnford Court yesterday, that Markland and Meiklam had no objection to a leetle snug speculation.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (with rising indignation) Then you fancied wrong, sir, and you may quote my contradiction to the next city gossip who takes liberties with our firm, (rings bell, R.) Markland and Meiklam have nothing to say to schemes or schemers. Leave my house, sir !

div.stage: Enter Servant, L. 3 E.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: You'll be sorry for this, Mr. Markland, and when the Great Metropolitan Cold Water Heating and Oxygenated Respiration Company is in its blaze of triumph, you'll regret this morning's work. It'll be too late then, Mr. Markland. (Servant holds door open, L.) I'm going, young man ! (turns) By the way I never mentioned my Anglo Indian Steam-Ginning Company— (checked by Markland, who pauses in his angry walk) Oh, don't be alarmed, I'm not the man to force anything on anybody. You're decided finally about "The Great Metropolitan ? " (Markland approaches almost fiercely) Oh, very well, very well! Good morning !

div.stage: (exit cheerfully but precipitately, D. L. 3. E., followed by Servant.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: At last! I couldn't have controlled my boot five minutes longer. The impudent charlatan, to mix my name up with questionable speculations! I must take measures to trace these reports home. I've returned just in time, (changing his tone) Yet perhaps the worst thing one can do with such stories is to notice them.

div.stage: Enter Servant, L. 3 E.

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.p: Mr. Meiklam, sir.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Show him in directly. Meiklam must know of these rumours. He should have warned me they were afloat. He has had carte blanche, almost, since my marriage. However, I assume the reins after to-day.

div.stage: Enter Meiklam, l.. 3 E., rather sanctimonious in appearance, cool, fresh, and collected.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (R.) Well?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p:
(l.) Very well, thank heaven! a beautiful
morning. We ought to be very thankful. I quite enjoyed my little walk over the bridge. You seem feverish.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Feverish ? No, only a little excited.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Excited ! That's not business like.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I've just had a fellow here—a promoter— Rocket.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (looking at card) I know the person.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And he has dared, on the strength of some idle gossip, to mix our name up with questionable speculations. I couldn't contradict him as explicitly as I should have liked to do.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: So you got into a passion, (sits l. c.) It's not a bad plan. I wish I was more easily excited sometimes.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: It was foolish, I admit I suppose, my father's grave did utter forth a voice ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Ah, your excellent father—what would he have thought of these days of limited liability and unlimited speculation! He was caution personified.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Say integrity.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: The most upright of men, and the most punctual of bankers. What would he have thought if anyone had told him of his son taking half a year's honeymoon instead of returning to the bank like a short bill, one month after date.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I'm afraid I've thrown a great deal on your shoulders.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Particularly as you were moving about so much, and in such out-of-the-way places. It was impossible to keep you even informed of operations, much less to consult you about them. But youth will be youth. I made allowances.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I must make up for it now by working double tides. I'm glad you've called : you can give me a bird's eye view of the last six months' operations, as we drive into town, (rises.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I thought it was as well to see you, as some little explanation might be necessary, which had better take place here than in the bank parlour.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Quite right. It would never do to expose my ignorance before old Scratchell. (sits.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Exactly, and then if there should be any item of information not quite so pleasant as the rest—you see you are so excitable.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You have no bad news, I hope ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Bad news is a relative term. In such times as we have had you could hardly expect our money matters to go on as smoothly as your honeymoon.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Don't beat about the bush. Let me know the worst. Though I could have wished you had chosen any day but this for bad news. It's my wife's birthday.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Ah! it is settling day for the foreign account too, unluckily.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And likely to be a bad settlement for the bulls, Molesworth tells me. Happily we have not much to do with that.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Excuse me. We have a good deal more to do with it than I could wish.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: What do you mean ? You've not been operating on your own account ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Oh dear no, but I thought it expedient in the exercise of the discretion you left me—and trusting to the best private information—to try and recoup ourselves by winnings in foreign stock, for some rather heavy losses in foreign shares.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Shares, stocks! Speak out—you've been speculating and losing by your speculations.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Only when I was unfortunate in our investments. Wildman and Waters, the great contractors for foreign lines, opened a heavy account with us soon after you left. Their references were first-rate, their transactions enormous. Unluckily their capital wasn't quite on the scale of their transactions. They found it difficult to meet some heavy bills, owing to the unsettled state of the American market. They applied to me for temporary assistance——

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And you gave it!

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I was always of a confiding turn, and they offered ten per cent, for the accommodation. The difficulty recurred—of course I couldn't think of losing our first advances, so I extended their credit.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Good heavens! Then Rocket may have spoken the truth.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I shouldn't think it likely.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: He said these men are desperately involved.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Unfortunately that is true.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And their credit with us ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (unctuously) They have taken large advantage of my disposition to trust my fellow men.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: What is the total of our liabilities on their paper ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (rising) Meiklarn!

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Excluding the odd hundreds; that's about it.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: How came it you never told me this ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: How could I, when you would go to such out-of- the-way places ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Why it will swallow nearly every farthing of my private fortune!

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Unfortunately I have not that resource. Of coarse, the house couldn't submit to such a loss, so after an unsuccessful venture or two in the produce-market—that produce-market is so unprincipled—I tried foreign stocks.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: When was this ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Two accounts ago. Both settlements were against us, so I continued.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Why did you not tell me the worst after the first account ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I hoped the next account would make the worst better—but it hasn't. I couldn't in justice to the house allow matters to remain in such an unsatisfactory position.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: In fact you knew, that now I was returning to business, an explanation could no longer be evaded.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: That is a disagreeable way of putting it.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: It is the truth. The amount of your last losses depends on to-day's Settlement.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Yes: we must see our brokers at once. The account closes at 12. It's nearly that now.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p:
(stopping him and looking him in the face)
Meiklam, do you know I was warned against you, before I took you into partnership ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I dare say ; the world is so censorious, and my daily walk was a reproach to many.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: They said you were one of those masked depredators who make piety their picklock, and cant their chloroform. I did not believe them. I have been too credulous, and I see now I may have to atone terribly for my too ready trust. May heaven forgive you if, as I sadly fear, you have brought ruin on me and mine!

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Ruin! Surely I needn't impress upon you the immense difference between insolvency and ruin.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I can't see it.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: That's just what I complain of. Insolvency is not being able to pay—ruin is being known not to be able. That, I am happy to say, we are as far from as ever. If you would only put a good face on things ! Confidence, my dear Markland—confidence is the soul of bnsiness!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: What you would call confidence I should call lying.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: It doesn't make things better to give them ugly names. So order your brougham, and on our way to the City I'll explain to you a little operation of my own, which I hope may set us straight yet.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Hush ! my wife!—not a word before her.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Markland, from D. L.U. E., and Molesworth comes down from conservatory, c.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Good morning, Mr. Meiklam. (Molesworth and Meiklam shake hands) It's no use, Harry, Mr. Molesworth can't find Harrington. He says he and Belle have both disappeared in the grounds.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: It's just as well: she would have spiked my guns. I have an appointment with the youngster, and when I do get within lecturing range—but come, Markland, I shall be late at Lincoln's Inn.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Very sorry, but here's my partner laid hands on me.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Oh, I wouldn't for worlds——

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Not the least consequence—drop me at the first cab-stand. (Meiklam and Molesworth retire up.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: But you're going out, darling ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, Mrs. Vernon has promised to take me a drive.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: That's right. Be very happy till I return. Come. (to Meiklam.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Good-bye, Mrs. Markland; you have a perfect paradise here.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Minus the serpent, I hope.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (aside) No; he's there too. Come, I say. (impatiently, going L. 3 E.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Harry! (ruefully) You're going without giving me a kiss.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (returning) My own darling,—heaven bless and protect you. (kisses her affectionately, and exit D. L. 3 E.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Till you come back ! I don't want any protector when you are here.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (reprovingly) Hush, my dear Mrs. Markland, I'm afraid that's rather an unchristian sentiment.

div.stage: (exit Meiklam, followed by Molesworth, L. 3 E)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I don't like the feel of that man's hand, it is like touching an earth worm—I'm certain he's a hypocrite, yet my husband trusts him. Dear Harry ! he looked pale and anxious. I hope Mr. Meiklam hasn't been worrying him.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Vernon, D. 3 L.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Now darling, ready ? Oh, yes, that is quite a lovely bonnet too!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I'm so glad you like it. (looks in the glass) Now to face my rival, L. S. D. (coquetishly) After all, I don't think I feel so much afraid of her.

div.stage: (go up together C.)

SCENE —The broker's office of Fermor and Laxton, stock-brokers, looking into Capel Court. Along the R. from the back to the first entrance, stand three Clerks' desks, set across from R. to L., within a mahogany partition with rails at the top. At the ends of the partition, nearest to and farthest from the audience, and thus opposite the first and third of these desks, are slabs for writing at, with pads, pens, and ink. Rows of pegs on walls with stock receipts attached, and papers in bundles, and in partition pigeon-holes for delivering and receiving stock papers, cheques, &c. Entrance to the office, R. 1 E., by glazed door. Umbrella stand and mat near it. At the back, in flat, a large window, transparent, commanding a view of Capel Court, and the entrance door of the Stock Exchange, so that when door is open the Stock Exchange Porter is seen in his place, and groups near him. L. 3 and 1 E., the doors communicating (L. 3 E.) with Fermor's private room, and (L. 1 E.) with Laxton's. Fixed upon the wall, between the two doors, is a clock. C, half-way up the stage, a handsome stove. Chairs R. and L. of the window, and on either side of door into private room. A screen, folded, standing against the wall between the two doors. As the curtain rises the business of the office is seen in full activity. A Client is writing out cheque at the first slab, another Client is transacting business at the upper pigeon-hole, another is handing in a bundle of stock receipts to one of the Clerks who has come out of the partition to examine them. Four Clerks are writing or running to and fro with books inside the partition. Fermor is conversing with a person who carries prospectuses at the door of his private room. Prospectus-Monger leaves him when curtain rises, both coming down. Fermor has a list in his hand.

sp.speaker: Prospectus-Monger.
sp.p: Then you say "no" definitely, Mr. Fermor ?

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: Decidedly—good morning, (exit Prospectus-Monger, R. 1 E., taking umbrella) Mr. Martin, (reading off from his list) three hundred Venezulans, for money, fifty Confederates, forty Buenos Ayres sixes, (exit Customer, R. 1 E., who was at lower pigeon-hole, having paid a cheque) six hundred Spanish New Deferreds, for next account.

sp.speaker: 1st Clerk.
sp.p: (coming out with his hat on, and with his note-book in which he has made the entry) Yes, sir.

div.stage: (exit Martin)

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: How are Buffalo and Lake Hurons ?

sp.speaker: 2nd Clerk.
sp.p: Last business done at five, sir. (Fermor makes a note.)

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: We've an order for sixty when they touch four three-eights, (exit Client who was at upper pigeon-hole) Did you see Mr. Laxton in the house ?

sp.speaker: 2nd Clerk.
sp.p: He hadn't come when I looked in last.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: (looking at his watch) He's late this morning, (exit Customer, R. 1 E., who was with Clerk near stove, Clerk re-enters partition) even for him. (to himself) Have you made up Mr. Meiklam's account for the settlement ?

sp.speaker: 2nd Clerk.
sp.p: Meiklam senior ? There it is, sir. (delivers it from lower pigeon-hole, Fermor takes it.)

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: (shaking his head as he looks at it) A heavy figure on the wrong side. Go and see if Mr. Laxton's in the house, and beg him to step over as soon as possible.

div.stage: (exit 2nd Clerk, R. 1 E.)
Enter a brother Broker, who just shows his head at the door, R. 1 E.

sp.speaker: Broker.
sp.p: Got any money ?

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: How much ?

sp.speaker: Broker.
sp.p: Three—till to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: Cheque, Mr. Martin! (Broker goes to lower pigeon-hole and waits till a cheque is handed out to him— Fermor takes it as he passes, reads and calls) Three fifteen!

div.stage: Enter Client with stock receipts, Client passes up to lower pigeon-hole and waits till No. 1 gets cheque and exit, then puts in his receipt and waits.
Enter Molesworth, R. 1 E.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Mr. Fermor.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: (comes down) Ah, Mr. Molesworth! We don't often see you in the city, sir.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Not so near Capel-court, at all events; I seldom get even so far as Garraway's.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: (rubbing his hands cheerfully) Can we do anything for you to-day ? It's a capital time for buying in: consols must go up with this fine harvest weather.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: No thank you, these are not times to put up with 3½ per cent., even at 88. I've called by appointment with my ward, Harrington, to see about settling for him, silly fellow; I wish he'd kept as clear of the Stock Exchange as I have.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: Boys will be boys—they must pay for their experience, (to clerk within partition) Mr. Harrington's account, Jackson. But that's Laxton's affair. He takes the fast men. I only transact for our steady customers. People must have occupation for their minds and their money.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: And gambling grows respectable, I suppose, when it's called business.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: Gambling! Oh, don't say that, Mr. Molesworth. Whatever Laxton's may be, mine is quite an investing connection.

div.stage: Enter Customer, R. 1 E.

sp.speaker: Customer.
sp.p: Mr. Fermor ?

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: Walk into my private room, sir. (exit Customer to Fermor's room L. U. E.) If you'll take a chair and the Times for a moment 'till Laxton comes in—I've sent over to the house for him. (exit L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Don't mind me. (sits L) It will be all the worse for Master Harrington when he does come, (sits and takes paper.)

div.stage: Enter Rocket, very eager, with a bundle of prospectuses in hand.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Mr. Laxton within ?

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: No, sir.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Then I want to see Mr. Fermor. (affecting to look at his watch) I've an appointment.

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: He's engaged, sir; if you'll wait a moment.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Very unlucky, my minutes are half-crowns. If you'd just let these prospectuses lie about, (puts prospectuses down here and there) Sow broadcast and something may come up. Ah! (recognising Molesworth) my dear Mr. Molesworth—(cordially) this is a most fortunate rencontre.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (looking up surprised) Sir!

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Rocket, my dear sir; you know, (gives card) Tom Rocket! Three times last week I called upon you to transact the legal business of a few first-class companies which I amuse myself by promoting.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Ah, I understand: I don't do that style of business, sir. (resumes his paper.)

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: That style of business, my dear sir! That is, not the ordinary bubble company scheme business—of course you do not, or I should not have come to you, I promise you: but the style of business which I have the honour to introduce to you is not that style of business. First and foremost here is the New Patent Traction Company, for applying the immense latent powers of the Trinidad oil wells to the acceleration of British traffic. I've the banker's name and the solicitor's still open. Of the solicitor's berth I mean to give you the refusal.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: That you can have at once.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: The name ? Thank you.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: No, the refusal.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (pausing, pen in hand) Don't be hasty, my dear sir! I can't afford to be hasty: I'm obliged to be so particular. You see I had filled up the banker's name with a first-class house, (shows prospectus.)

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I see, Markland and Meiklam.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Reputed A 1—reputed—but you will observe I have struck my pen through the name.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: So I see—I'll thank you to do as much for mine. I suppose, like me, they gave you a refusal.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: No, sir, I gave them one. The bank that is associated with any company of mine must be, like Caesar's wife, above suspicion. Now M. and M., between ourselves are—in the language of the City—fishy.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Take care, sir, or you may be exposing yourself to an action of defamation.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Pooh, my dear sir, I'm obliged to be familiar with everything that is shaky in the money world.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I can easily understand that.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: And do you mean to tell me that a bank which is mixed up with one of the most desperate concerns in the market—Rocky-mountain Grand Trunks —

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Why you don't mean to say that Markland and Meiklam have to do with that bankrupt speculation ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: If you're interested in their solvency, make inquiries, my dear sir, satisfy yourself, only don't mention my name, (going up to Clerk) Would you remind Mr. Fermor I'm waiting, and take him this ? (writes at slab.)

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (coming forward) And I left orders to pay in that forty thousand this morning, and they've Harrington's securities in their hands too, to more than that amount! This fellow's news takes my breath away! Mine's quite a family connection. I'm a mere baby in this world of speculation. But it can't be true. He gets his livelihood by lying, (exit Clerk into Fermor's room, with note, L. 3 E.) Still there can be no harm in inquiry. This may be very important to me, sir. Can you prove what you have said ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: With the greatest ease—if it were worth my while.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: It shall be.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Confidence respected, of course ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Naturally, — a privileged communication. When and where will you meet me with proofs ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: At your office at three.

div.stage: Re-enter Clerk, from Fermor's room L. 2. E.

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: Mr. Fermor says he's engaged, sir.

div.stage: Enter Harrington, R. 1 E.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Mr. Laxton ?

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: He'll be in directly, sir.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Here's my scapegrace—not a word to him of this till his money's safe. So, sir

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (coming forward, seeing Molesworth) I hope I haven't kept you waiting, sir.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: You have, sir, but I can charge for that. What you can't pay me for is the anxiety, the pain you have given me by your folly—your gambling.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Gambling, sir?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Yes, sir, gambling. When you risk your money on a chance you can't control, I don't see that it matters much whether it's on the turn of a die, or the see-saw of a time-bargain.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Well, but, sir, you always said you wished I had some business—I wasn't brought up to any. Time-bargains wanted no training. Lots of fellows I knew were going in for them, so I went in too. I thought it was rather the steady thing than not.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: And you've lost £700 !

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: No end of fellows at the club have made lots of money at this work.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Did you ask about the losers ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (ruefully) I suppose they kept dark.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (coming forward) Excuse my interrupting you, but as I gather that this gentleman has money, and wants occupation, suppose I provided him with light and remunerative employment as a director of my companies—fee a guinea a meeting,—entre nous, no difficulty about qualification—I think I've a seat or two still open, on the Hydrostatic Plank.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Thank you; at present he's only gulling himself—as one of your directors, he might be gulling the public.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p:
Gulling? Oh, sir, there are few gulls have
been more cruelly plucked than I was. Yes, my young friend, you see before you a sad warning. I started in life with a nice little fortune—I speculated for the account as you've been doing

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: And lost, as he's been doing ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (sadly) No, that was the devil of it. I won; and then I went on and lost, and then I won again, and so up and down, bull and bear, till between the brutes I was plucked of every feather, and waddled out of the house a lame duck!

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (to Harrington) You see, sir ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (gradually recovering his elasticity) And then I discovered my true vocation. The rapid coup d'oeil—the sanguine temperament—that had me a rash speculator, turned in the channel of promotion, produced the brilliant inventor, the energetic fosterer of great ideas, the influential medium between floating capital and industrial enterprise whom you see before you. Avoid speculation, my young friend, and invest your money in well-considered undertakings. Here are a few of mine to choose from, (taking out prospectuses.)

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Mr. Rocket, if this young gentleman is bent on going to the dogs, at least allow him to find his own way to the kennel.

div.stage: Enter Customer, from Fermor's room, and goes off, R. 1 E., the moment Fermor's door is opened Rocket dashes at it as Fermor appears at the door.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Fermor! Ten minutes, my dear sir. Good morning (to Molesworth and Harrington) —you may as well keep those prospectuses. You can lay them on your club table: pleasant and profitable reading —calculated to inspire a taste for investment, and a wholesome horror of speculation.

div.stage: (exit Rocket into Fermor's room.)

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Now does that fellow really believe in himself, or only wish to make us believe in him ? Of all the knotty points I come across, there's none so difficult as to determine, in these cases, the exact proportions of knave and fool, (takes a pinch of snuff.)

div.stage: Enter Laxton and Frank Meiklam, in animated conversation, R. 1. E.

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: Well, but look here, Franky, the Nobbler can't stand up to him for six rounds.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: I bet you a hat on the event.

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: Done with you, sir. Ah, Harrington. (Frank goes up familiarly to Harrington, who acknowledges his greeting stiffly) And Mr. Molesworth! Who would have thought of seeing you in Capel Court.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Thank you, I've called about this gentleman's account: good morning, Mr. Meiklam.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Quite gives us a touch of the respectable, sir, to have you among us.

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: Speak for yourself, Franky. Give me Mr. Harrington's account, Martin, and (referring to list) book eighty Lundys, fifty Cachars, thirty Mariquitas, and hundred Great Souths to Mr. Meiklam. (L., up at pigeon-hole.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Mr. Frank Meiklam, Martin. The old boy's got an account here, too, and I don't want any mistake.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Your transactions seem extensive, young gentleman, for a bank clerk.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Clerk ? Oh, I'm like the Emperor of the French, the nephew of my uncle. I mean to be a partner one of these days if I find it worth my while, so, till the old boy proposes it, I do a little private business on my own account—in the City Punting Club as I call it. Jack here's my coxswain, to steer me well on the flats.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Steer you clear of them, I suppose you mean ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: No, no, sir, in Capel Court punting a good shallow flat is the very thing we look out for—a green soft place to shoot stock that won't float; that's our little game, sir.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (sternly) And is your uncle aware of this little game of yours ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: He's too wide awake to ask questions. He treats me with confidence, and takes it out in affection.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (dryly) Hard to say which has the best of the bargain!

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: (coming down) Here's Mr. Harrington's account, seven hundred and fifty on the wrong side.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Fishy!

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (putting up account) I'll send you a cheque for it.

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: And here you are, Mr. Franky, three hundred to the good.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Not bad for a fortnight's work in fancy lots, eh, Mr. Molesworth ? Keeps a fellow in gloves. Ah, Harrington, my boy, you should let me tool you through the market. (Laxton goes into Clerks' partition, R.)

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Thank you, he's going to leave the punting club.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: If he can't handle his pole better, it's just as well.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Let me give you a bit of advice.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: You won't charge six-and-eightpence for it ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: And you won't expect me to take it ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I'm afraid not.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Then you may give it me.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: You'd better leave the punting club too.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: I say, Jack! (over his shoulder to Laxton) Here's Mr. Molesworth wants me to go in for steady, sober, mill-horse money-grubbing—No thank you, Mr. Molesworth, they breed a faster style of animal now, sir, than they did in your day. We start for the Great Metropolitan Stakes, across country—plough or pasture, bull finch or post and rail, water or timber—harden your heart, hustle your horse, and never say die! It's pace that wins, and pluck that carries you over.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (aside, turning in disgust) What an ineffable snob!

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Mercy on us! This boy takes my breath away! I feel like a fossil in a cutting, with the express dashing by

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Of course, I mean to pull up when I've made a pot—marry and come the respectable dodge.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (drily) You're wife'll be a very enviable woman.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Yes, I don't think she'll have a bad bargain—I've the party in my eye. She's a friend of yours, by-the-bye, and if you like to be one of my references to character——

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I never commit myself——

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Not that I think Miss Hargreave will want references.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (coming down) I think, Mr. Meiklam, the less ladies' names are mentioned the better.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Oh, Jack's tiled. By the way, you know Miss Hargreave ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Yes, and for that reason I must insist on her name not being made so free with in a place like this.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (sneeringly) Her name's as safe in my hands as in yours, I should think, (turning, catches sight through glazed door) Hallo! that's Markland's brougham—our governor's, by Jingo! They mustn't catch me here. Don't peach, Mr. Molesworth. (exit hastily with Laxton into Laxton's room, L. 3 E.)

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (aside and suspiciously) Brokers should go to bankers, not bankers come to brokers—it looks ugly!

div.stage: Enter Markland and Meiklam, R. 1 E.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (impetuously) Mr. Fermor ?

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: Name, sir ?

div.stage: (Meiklam wipes his feet very carefully on mat.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (writes at slab and folds up paper) Give him that.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: How this city mud sticks—merely walking across the pavement—yet one gets one's boots soiled!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Hardly worth while being so particular about your boots, when your hands——

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (coughs significantly) Ah, Mr. Molesworth—and my young friend, Mr. Harrington!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (embarrassed) Molesworth, you here ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: If you'd told me you were coming, you might have brought me.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: So I might, but I had no idea when you called at Putney—

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (slyly) Investing—I suppose—for a client ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: And you, no doubt, for a customer. We have both kept our secret. I had fancied the etiquette was for the brokers to come to the bank parlours.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: As a general rule, but there are exceptions.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (dryly) So I see.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (interrupting) By the way, I want you to write to your friend Hookham: on second thoughts I think I'd better decline the borough.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Indeed.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Oh, I'm so sorry! Ah, Mr. Molesworth, the House of Commons is the true arena for the British capitalist. If I had had Markland's early advantages—but I'm a self-made man! (humbly) I hope I have made the best of the talent entrusted to me.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: The world gives you full credit for it, Meiklam.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (with feverish gaiety) Of course you're both coming to us to-night: we shall be such a gay party—ball and concert, and fireworks on the lawn, and Gunter only knows what a supper! It's my wife's birthday, you know.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I'll try and look in. Good morning. Come, George, (crosses R.)

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (shaking hands with Markland) Of course you may count on me. I've engaged Miss Hargreave for the first deux temps, this morning, (follows Molesworth.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Ah, young man, may you learn to employ your season of youth more profitably!

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Amen to your little sermon, Mr. Meiklam there's nothing like preaching by example.

div.stage: (exeunt Molesworth and Harrington, R.)
Fermor appears at the door of his room, L. 2, E.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: (to CLERK) The file of prospectuses for 1862. I'll see you, gentlemen, as soon as I get rid of this very troublesome customer.

div.stage: Fermor retires, L. 2 E., Clerk takes in the file, L. 2 E., leaving office empty of clerks.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: We're alone now.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: So we were all the drive from Putney. I was most explicit, but I couldn't get a word out of you; it was almost offensive.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Can't you guess why I was silent ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I hope at least your thoughts were profitably employed.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I was silent, for fear I should speak my mind.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Isn't that just what partners owe to each other ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Shall I speak now ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: If it would be any comfort to you.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I felt all the while as a lost soul might feel by the side of his destroyer. All this half year since my marriage—while I was caressing my happiness at home—you, in your desperate haste to be rich, were sowing the seeds of ruin broadcast—you flung good money after bad, till every legitimate resource was exhausted, and now you have crowned your work! Your last wild ventures yonder— (pointing through window to Stock Exchange)—have landed us in a loss that must bring us to the Gazette!

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (resignedly) This is very hard; but I will remember my privileges and try not to resent it. (sits.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Resent it! Is it not true—true, every word ? What was the position of the bank, when I raised you from cashier to partner, as my father had raised you from clerk to cashier ? You found the firm rich, honoured, honourable. What will the world call it to-morrow ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (holding up his hands) And this is the return for the employment of my talent! Mr. Markland, I would blush for you, were I not sure that, in your cooler moments, you will blush for yourself.

div.stage: Re-enter Clerk from Fermor's room, L. 2 E., followed by Rocket—Fermor appears at the door behind him.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: It will float, my dear sir, depend upon it, it will float. I only want my corks in the shape of six weighty directors.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: Now, gentlemen ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Meiklam—Mr. Markland! (turning to Fermor) Mr. Markland and I had a long and pleasant interview this morning, (to Markland, aside) I hope you have thought better of the Associated Cold Water. (Markland shakes Rocket off, and passes after Meiklam into Fermor's room, L. 2 E.) Cold water with a vengeance! (to Clerk) The governor seems mightily taken with that Hydrostatic Plank. I shall have filled up my directors, say the day after to-morrow, and by next account day I shall have touched six thousand promotion money—I let 'em off easy you see. Now for a chop at Dolly's, eh ? (feeling in porte-monnaie) I've nothing less than a fiver about me., (to Clerk) I say, could you let me have one-and-six ? I shall be passing this way in an hour.

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: Hadn't you better make it even money, Mr. Rocket ? Have a florin.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Thank you, perhaps I had. (takes it, aside) That's two chops. I say, Martin, don't forget I've a few chairs vacant, if you come across a likely director. Of course I should make it worth your while—nice little douceur—say twenty per chair—(aside) In shares, of course.

div.stage: (exit Rocket, R. 1. E.)

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: Poor devil, he's to be pitied!

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Vernon and Mrs. Markland, R. 1. E.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Here we are at last. Mr. Laxton ?

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: In his room, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Take my card. (Clerk goes into Laxton's room, L. 3 E.) Well, my dear, and what do you say of the city now ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: My brain's in a whirl. Such narrow streets —such a crush of traffic—such dingy windows—and such jostling crowds—and all apparently in such a hurry!

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Yes, my dear, they can't afford to dawdle. Some are trying to catch Time by the forelock, and you know he won't stop for any man, and others to catch Mammon by the tail, and he's a very slippery customer.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Surely it can't be very wholesome to breathe this air every day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p:
It's apt to give people a very dangerous
complaint—money on the brain. I've had a touch of it myself.

div.stage: Re-enter Clerk, L. 3 E.

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: Mr. Laxton will see you in a moment, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: (to Mrs. Markland) If you'll sit down here, my love, while I'm with my broker: you may take the Times and peep from behind it at all that goes on.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, pray don't be long! I begin to feel, somehow, as if I had done wrong in coming.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Pooh, pooh! (Laxton's door L. 3. E., opens, Laxton and Frank appear, they exchange vulgar dumb show at sight of the ladies.)

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: (politely) I am quite at your service, Mrs. Vernon. (she goes in—Frank comes down.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: By Jove! Mrs. Markland!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Mr. Meiklam!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Well, this is an unexpected pleasure, (goes to pigeon-hole.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, I came with— (aside) No, I promised not to mention her name.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (who has got a cheque at the pigeon-hole) Yes, you came with ——?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, it's no one you know, I think.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Oh, then you didn't come with Markland ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: My husband—oh, no!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Then you were not aware—I mean he's not aware—that you are here ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (confused, but recovering herself) Really, Mr. Meiklam, this kind of cross questioning——

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (with offensive discretion) Oh, Mrs. Markland, a lady's secret is perfectly safe in my hands.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But I have no secret, Mr. Meiklam.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Of course if a lady likes to do a little speculation out of her pin money——

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Pray understand, Mr. Meiklam, that I am here for nothing of the kind, (aside) Oh, if Mrs. Vernon would but come ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: By the way, allow me to wish you many happy Returns of the day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (confused) Thank you.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: You see I know it's your birthday—though you forgot to send me a card for the fête.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (embarrassed) I'm very sorry. I ought to have done so—pray come.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (going up to the slab and writing) That means "go! " (aside) I won't let her off so easy. Now I call this very pleasant—almost as pleasant as cold shoulder at Putney, (comes down) Thank you! Look, I've filled up an invitation. "Mrs. Markland particularly requests the pleasure of Mr. Frank Meiklam's company at the Rosary, Putney, on Friday, the 25th. Dancing." I've dated it last week, that when I stick it over my mantelpiece nobody may see how you've neglected me. (Mrs. Markland signs it.)

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: (from the door. L. 3 E.) Mrs. Vernon's account, Martin. (Clerk goes in with it, L. 3 E.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Now you've trusted me with your secret you put me on the footing of a friend at once.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Mr. Meiklam, that's the second time you've used the word secret; be good enough not to repeat it—I have no secret to conceal from my husband—if I had, I should not choose you for my confidant.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Thank you! good morning. But before I go, I think, as you are here on the sly—

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (rising with dignity) Mr. Meiklam, it should be enough to protect me from such an insinuation that I am here alone.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: At least you have a protector very near at hand —your husband is in that room. (pointing to Fermor's door) Of course there's no harm in your being here, but I thought you might like to know. There's nothing I enjoy so much as giving my friends agreeable surprises.

div.stage: (exit Frank, R. 1 E.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p:
Harry in that room! Perhaps he won't like my coming here without telling him—I know so little about these things—then my promise to Mrs. Vernon! How I wish she would come, and we might slip away at once. How annoying that young Mr. Meiklam should have
found that I was here without my husband's knowledge! There was something intolerable in the way he looked and spoke. I can't bear anyone should imagine I could have a secret from Harry, and he least of all—and why should I ? I'll tell Harry I came with a friend, but that I promised not to name her, and he won't ask, I'm sure —he will trust me, as I would trust him. We have not had one secret from each other since we married, and I hope we never shall, (door of Fermor's room opens) Hark! I hear his voice. How silly to put myself in this flutter.
