I'll tell him at once! No, I'll give him a surprise, and pop upon him as he comes out. Oh, it will be such fun! (overflowing with suppressed enjoyment and expectation she stands behind the door, which conceals her as it opens) Here he comes!

div.stage: Enter, D. L. 2 E., Markland, in a state of collapse, followed by Fermor, and Meiklam making an entry in his note-book—she is preparing to show herself suddenly to Markland when she sees the others.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: He is not alone! (drawing back.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (reading in his note-book) Thirty-nine thousand seven hundred and eighty, nineteen and six. You shall have a cheque, Mr. Fermor.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: If you please, Mr. Meiklam. It's a large sum, and runs over three accounts, as you're aware.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I hope we have not inconvenienced you. Good morning, Mr. Fermor—our cheque shall be to hand before you close for the day.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: I thank you, Mr. Meiklam. (cheerfully) Now it's all over—I may tell you, gentlemen, I was a leetle fidgetty.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (eagerly) What do you mean ?

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: Unpleasant reports arising out of your connection with that unlucky American contract—not that I ever gave any belief to them.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p:
Of course not—pray contradict anything of the kind. Our good name, Mr. Fermor—I am speaking for Mr. Markland as well as for myself—is to us a pearl of
price (with dignity) and he that sullies it must be prepared for exemplary damages.

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: And serve him right too. But I've my fortnight's balance sheet to make up—I'm sure you'll excuse me, gentlemen. (returns into his room L. 2 E.)

div.stage: (Mrs. Markland prepares to come out, but is checked by the tone of Markland's voice.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Now, sir, is the farce played out ? Is it time to take off our masks and face the truth, although the truth be ruin?

div.stage: (Mrs. Markland's expression of face should be a running comment on the dialogue which follows.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: What do you mean by this dreadful language ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Even your ingenuity cannot longer make head against our desperate circumstances. The last fortnight's mad game has gone against you—the stakes must be paid to-day. Where are we to find the means ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: And all this excitement for a paltry forty thousand pounds!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: In our position it might as well be ten times forty, from what you have yourself shown me. We cannot raise this money: it is impossible.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Oh, my young friend, remember Napoleon, and erase that feeble word from your vocabulary. Leave me to find the funds.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: On one condition.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: You'll allow me a margin of ten percent, above the bank rate ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: That you raise them by means that will not involve our—my honor. If I must sink it shall be with an unstained flag still flying over the wreck as I go down.

div.stage: (crosses L.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: What a beautiful sentiment for a winding up meeting!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p:
Yet to bring ruin home with me! To bid that grim guest sit down between me and my young wife, by the fireside that has been so bright, in her presence that is so loving and so trustful, and, till it comes, to have to keep the terrible secret even from her
who confides all to me! Oh, that I had never lived to see this day.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (at the door, speaking off—calling) Turn the horse's head, my man. (to Markland) This is flying in the face of Providence. I don't exactly see how at this moment, but I am satisfied I shall raise the money. But then I have faith—faith, my dear Markland!

div.stage: (exit Meiklam followed by Markland, R. 1 E.—Mrs. Markland stands as if paralysed, tries to speak and follow her husband, but her voice fails her and she has to support herself by a chair.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Ruin—he said ruin! Ruin! and I, in my senseless security, wished for it, only this morning! I did not think what it meant then—I seem to understand it now—the black shadow falling on our happy home, and darkening our lives that seemed all sunshine. No more sun for us now! (takes out her handkerchief, dropping her portemonnaie) No more? has money made our happiness? or anything that money can buy or bring ? He has been all to me, now is the time for me to be more to him than ever. I did not think I could love him more, but now I feel as if my love could grow and grow! I can be of use now! Oh yes, if heaven will but give me the power to comfort him, and turn the weakness of my woman's heart to strength for him to lean upon!

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Vernon cheerfully from Laxton's office, L.U. E.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Now dear, I've had a most successful settlement, and I mean to indulge myself with a new dress, so come, (crosses R.) let's have a delightful long morning turning over the moires at Marshall's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (turning to her with an effort) I'm quite ready (tries to follow her, but staggers and all but faints; Mrs. Vernon startled turns and supports her—tableau.)

div.stage: Act Drop—(Quickly.)

div.head: THE BANK PARLOUR.
div.stage: SCENE. —A handsome old-fashioned oak panelled room. Two long windows, R., with faded morone curtains, old Turkey carpet, mahogany chairs with morocco leather. In the panelling portraits of former partners. Bureau between windows, R. C., with directory, red book, and writing materials. Library table, C. Door leading to outer office, L. 2 E. Door to strong room in flat, L. C. Door in flat, R., communicating with private staircase. Old-fashioned oak fire-place in C. flat, with painting in the Jacobean style.
Meiklam discovered, he has been examining the year's accounts: the bank books are beside him, one on the table, others on the floor; he closes a book.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: A most satisfactory balance-sheet,—if all the bills entered to credit were good, and so long as the bad debts are kept out of this highly indiscreet record, (laying his hand on book) and confined to my little private friend here, (tapping a small green book.) Enter Scratchell, L. 2 E. I've done with the books, Scratchell, and I must say they reflect infinite crediton all concerned, (Scratchell bows) of which you are entitled to the lion's share. You will have your reward, Scratchell,—I do not mean merely in a handsome douceur at Christmas, but here, (touches his heart) and there! (points upwards, Scratchell bows but lingers) You have something to say to me ? Speak freely (unctuously)—our clerks' interests, still more our cashier's, are our own.

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: It's about Mr. Frank, Mr. Meiklam, though it's hardly my business, perhaps ——

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Speak out, Scratchell: truth is a duty we owe to ourselves, even if we did not owe it to our employers.

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: He's sadly irregular in his attendance—out now—(Meiklam sighs and shakes his head) and then how out of his salary he can keep horses, and dress as he does—and what business those ladies in pink bonnets and broughams have leaving little cocked hat notes for him—

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Spare me the revolting details! My own nephew, brought up with Christian privileges, and under my own eyes! Send him to me when he comes in, Scratchell. By the way, Scratchell, any heavy payments in this morning ?

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: Yes, sir, £40,000 trust money of young Harrington's to Mr. Molesworth's account, not half an hour ago.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (starting, but recovering himself) On second thoughts—you can leave the books, (exit Scratchell, L. 2 E.) My faith never failed me ! How the wind is tempered to the shorn lamb! This forty thousand will just stop the gap. Enter Messenger, L. 2 E., gives card. Rocket! It was who he dared to repeat these city scandals. I'll see him, (exit Messenger, L. 2 E.) and teach him (sternly) that the good name of a firm like ours is not to be calumniated with impunity. Enter Rocket, L. 2 E. Harkye, Mr, Rocket, it's lucky for you you are not worth powder and shot, or I might have to bring you to legal account for daring to impugn the credit of our house, sir.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: I, Mr. Meiklam ? I only alluded to your being heavily engaged with Wildman and Waters. It would give me pleasure to deny any report to the disadvantage of an old friend.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: An old friend!

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: We were flogged through the propria quoe maribus together—and you know I advanced all the funds for our first joint speculation.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: And what of that, sir ? It failed.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: But somehow you came safe out of the mess. Not that I blame you for that—but I was able to help you then, and I want help sadly now.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Pshaw, the old story !

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: NO ! I've a lot of things coming out, excellent things, some of them really likely to float, and if they do, safe to bring me home handsomely.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: You may spare this moonshine with me.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: No, really, matters never were so bright with me—in prospect. But you know the labour it takes to start a thing, and, en attendant, I'm actually in want of a few pounds,—it seems ridiculous, but it's a fact. Mrs. Rocket and two of the babes are down in the scarlet fever, poor things, and when I ran home to look after 'em just now, I found a note from the landlord threatening to put an execution in the house. I've offered him scrip in the Hydrostatic Plank, when it comes out,—but he doesn't see it.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: And I don't see it either. Mr. Rocket, you have already made several attacks on my purse. I trust it will never be closed against the really deserving poor, but if you want assistance you had better go to some firm that is not mixed up with Wildman and Waters.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (very eagerly) I'll contradict the report to everybody I've mentioned it to, if you'll only help me this once. If you could see them at home—the children are so ill:—there's my Bob,—such a sweet fellow

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Once for all, sir, I have nothing for you !

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (changing his tone) Take care, Mr. Meiklam, yon may repent this.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: A threat! Go away, sir, go away !

div.stage: Enter Molesworth, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (rising and crossing to Molesworth) Ah, Mr. Molesworth.! I've nothing to say to you, Mr. Rocket!

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p:
But I've something to say to Mr. Molesworth, (aside to Molesworth) I've great pleasure in handing you those proofs I promised, (gives papers) I say, if you
could advance me a tenner on account of my fee for the information—

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: True, I promised to make it worth your while (gives note) There !

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Ah, ha, beef-tea and brandy ad libitum— powder for the little fireworks! (to Molesworth) God bless you, sir. (to Meiklam) Good morning, Mr. Meiklam. (to Molesworth) An old schoolfellow of mine, sir, I never shall forget what I owe him. (exit L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Sorry to see that leech has fastened on you, my dear sir. A loose, unprincipled man, Mr. Molesworth. I have reason to think,—it's hardly worth mentioning, perhaps—that he has been talking rather freely of our house.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Well, he did drop some hints that made me rather uncomfortable.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I am happy to have the means of setting you at your ease. I was just looking through the books. Here are our balance-sheets—(passing over sheets)—monthly, quarterly, half-yearly, and for the year! (Molesworth looks at them) Oh, examine them freely : I wish to have no secrets from so valued a customer.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I see, I see, quite regular ! Egad, you may be proud of showing such a balance, Mr. Meiklam.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (taking receipt from drawer of table) And there's our income-tax receipt! (hands it over) An eloquent little document that, Mr. Molesworth, which I should not show to everybody.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (looks at it) It would be well if everybody in Schedule D were as honest.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I have always made it a principle to debit ourselves to the uttermost farthing; it's a duty one owes to one's conscience.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: To say nothing of the commissioners. Well, this is most satisfactory, so I'll just draw a cheque for Laxton's account against that foolish fellow, Harrington. (writes cheque.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: What, a stock-jobbing debt—ah, this is very sad, very sad—the young men of the day, (shakes his head) I fear, have not that wholesome horror of speculation which in this Christian land ——

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (rising and taking his hat) Goes on about as briskly as if the Stock Exchange had been an apostolic institution. Christianity and cash seem to get along uncommonly well together. And now to examine Rocket's proofs. (exit L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: A worldly old man, but I think I've nipped his suspicions in the bud. (sees green book) He would not have liked the look of things here quite so well. I mustn't leave this lying about, (taking out a small key, goes up to strong-room, L. C.—as he enters it, and while his back is turned, enter Frank Meiklam, L. 2 E. ; he sees his uncle and watches him, carefully; the strong-room door being left open Meiklam is seen by his nephew to deposit his green ledger in a private drawer under the safe—Frank shows by his looks and gestures the importance he attaches to all this. As Meiklam locks the door and turns round his eye meets that of his nephew, he shows a momentary confusion, but it is at once repressed and uncle and nephew look at each other, each attempting to command the other's eye, but without effect—Meiklam comes down, R.) So, sir, you are here at last! Where have you been this morning ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Where I had the unexpected pleasure of seeing yon, sir—at Capel Court. It's very instructive down there, sir, don't you think so ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: If you go on in this way, young man, what do you expect to come to ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: A partnership!

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: A partnership ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Unless you marry and take to continuing the line of the Meiklams on your own hook. I suppose you'll prefer keeping the business in the family.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: What! admit into the house a young man of your loose life and unsettled opinions!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Oh, as for my loose life I can soon screw that up when I've an object in going steady; and as for my "unsettled opinions" I've an opinion quite settled that "money makes the man, " which I take it is about the best bankers' catechism going.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: A scoffer, too! Oh, what appeal can I make to this hardened heart!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Anything but "preachee preachee," uncle : that won't do me any good. Treat me as the costermongers do their donkeys, tie a carrot to the end of the pole : say "If you're steady for four mouths, six months, a-year, you shall have a junior partnership," and then see what a model young man I'll be.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Unhappy boy—impunity has made you bold, and you've been going downwards, downwards—

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (saucily) Like the cow's tail.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Take care, sir, even my patience has its limits, and my power to protect you has been strained to the utmost. The means for your profligate expenditure, sir— how are they accounted for ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Well, sir, it used to be billiards and a little book-making, but I'm in a far better line now—time bargains. I've won £300 the last account, sir; I don't mind telling you, because then you'll understand, if I do go the pace, it's not out of the till.

div.stage: Enter Scratchell, with note, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: A messenger from Mr. Markland.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Say I'll see him. (exit Scratchell, L. 2 E.) Sit down there, sir, (to Frank, sternly) and await my return. (exit Meiklam, L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: I wonder if the old boy knows I see through him ? He's lived on hypocrisy so long that perhaps it's really a comfort to him. When he comes the extra religious, I'm sure he always has some particularly sharp practice in his eye. He'll find I'm a match for him. Here's a set of duplicate keys I had made after his. What a flat to fall asleep after dinner, with me in the room! I've a curiosity about the contents of that little green book the old boy's so sweet on. I saw where he put it—so here goes, (steals up and unlocks strong room L. C. : is seen to unlock private, drawer under safe and take green book from it: as he is coming out with it the door, R. C. opens, and Markland enters: Frank hastily withdraws inside strong room and closes the door cautiously from within)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p:
Meiklam not here! (down R.) I have tried every source—every source that is honourable and
regular—without effect. We must go! It is hard! A fortune so laboriously reared! A firm so long respected —and all kicked down by one whom my father raised from nothing. I must share the blame, as I shall share the punishment.

div.stage: Enter Meiklam, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Meiklam.
sp.p: (L.) Now, sir! My nephew gone! Markland, I was just sending a line by your messenger.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: On second thoughts I determined to be the bearer of my own bad news. I have failed.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (sits) Ah, you would go about it. You are not the man for an emergency.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: When the emergency is to be met by fair means, yes; when by foul ones, no! (sits R.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: We won't bandy words. You have brought bad news; I have good news for you in return. I've found the money.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Where ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Molesworth has paid in £40,000 in the course of the morning. Just when you were flying in the face of Providence ! It should be a lesson to you!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And you mean to appropriate this payment ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Appropriate, my dear sir ? Bankers' deposits are not ear-marked; it can be replaced as easily as taken.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Out of the next customer's deposits to the same amount.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I will not be a partner in such rascality.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Unfortunately you are a partner already, and the world will saddle you with a joint responsibility for our operations.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: True, true !

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Besides, this little cloud will soon blow over, if you will leave me to raise the wind.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Tempter! And the reaping of the whirlwind ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Metaphors prove nothing. But I've taken your leave for granted. I've transferred that £40,000 to my private account.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Robber! (rises.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (rises) There, I'm glad you've said it! It's been on your mind all day, and you'll be better now you've got it out—I won't resent it: my faith teaches me forgiveness of injuries, (sits.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Robber and hypocrite !

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Go on! and when you've done abusing me, we'll come back to business.

div.stage: Enter Scratchell, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: Good morning, Mr. Markland, Mr. Molesworth would be particularly glad to see and speak with you.

div.stage: Enter Molesworth, followed by Rocket, L. 2 E., and exit Scratchell, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Ah, my dear sir, two visits in one morning! We are highly favoured.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Thank you. Ah, Markland, I've taken the liberty of bringing in a friend of mine.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: I know Mr. Meiklam is always glad to see his old schoolfellow.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: You may remember, my dear Markland, I ordered that £40,000 to be paid in this morning ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes, against my advice, you remember.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: True, you said you would rather not have the responsibility of such a heavy amount on call. Perhaps you've changed your mind ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: No, I'm more of that mind than ever. If you want to oblige me, Molesworth, you can't show it more than by drawing out this money.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (aside) Is he mad ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Here's a cheque-book,—draw at once.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Don't be in a hurry. Large interest means risky investment. My young friend here has the rashness of his years. Take an older man's advice, Mr. Molesworth, and leave your money where it is.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Take it out, I say, and do not listen to his cautious counsels.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I don't mind mentioning it now—but you're aware of some disagreeable reports affecting your firm ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes, yes!

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: And in the face of these reports I should have felt a delicacy in drawing out the money.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Oh, I waive that! I insist on your drawing it out—I will not he indebted even to your delicacy.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Oh, make your mind easy, Mr. Meiklam has satisfied me already that there was no foundation for these city scandals.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (with surprise) Oh, Meiklam has satisfied you of that ?

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Yes, by showing me your balance-sheet, and last income-tax receipt. My friend here has given me the choice of so many splendid investments, that the only difficulty is which to take.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: You see, gentlemen, Mr. Molesworth at least is not blind to his own interests.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: (having filled up cheque) There! (rising) I'll take the money as I go out. Good morning. Come, Mr. Rocket. (exit L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: (to Meiklam, as he is going out) A first instalment of my debt, Mr. Meiklam, but I've not done yet. (exit following Molesworth)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: There's one friend rescued at least.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: And to save your exaggerated susceptibilities you have precipitated, perhaps, the downfall of the firm! Why did you urge him to do this ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Because I prefer ruin to dishonour.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Oh, that was your reason. Then listen to me; if ruin comes, dishonour will come with it, even as it is. I showed him a balance-sheet, but I did not show him the balance-sheet.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: More villainy—I knew nothing of this.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Have you treated me in a way to invite confidence ? But will the world believe in your ignorance ? Hardly, my dear sir.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Meiklam, have a care—do not trifle with the misery you have wrought (restraining himself) No, no, spare me, man—spare me for my wife's sake, if not my own.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p:
My dear young friend, I am full of commiseration for both of you. But you see we can't afford to
bring our books into the bankruptcy court. This disappointment is awkward, but it may be repaired. We have marketable securities of Harrington's for twice as much. It would be so easy to get an advance on them. They're in the safe.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I know now you have no conscience, but have you no fear of the law ? Do you not see if what we have done be rash, reckless, wicked—that this would be criminal ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (at the strong room door) I can't get my key into the lock ! The wards have been tampered with. One moment—there's a locksmith a few doors off. (Meiklam hurries off L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Come what may, I will not consent to this new infamy. I have been weak, but my conscience is still pure. Even if the law's award and the world's opinion cover my name with infamy, I shall know my own hands are clean, and my Florry,—she at least will believe me when I tell her so.

div.stage: Enter Scratchell, L.

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: Mrs. Markland and Mrs. Vernon are at the private door, sir.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Then I will go to them, (exit Scratchell, L.) Thank heaven my wife knows nothing! May affection give me power still to wear a smile for her! (exit R. C. door.)

div.stage: Frank appears from the strong-room, L. C., the door which he relocks,

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: A capital idea, my plugging the keyhole. By Jove, this is what I call payment for peeping! (exit R. C. door.)

div.stage: Enter Miss Hargreave, followed by Laxton, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Neither my sister nor Markland here—our appointment was for three, sharp : so much for business punctuality, Mr. Laxton !

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: I wished particularly to see Mr. Meiklam, but I can't wait. It was lucky I met you, Miss Hargreave) you can give this to Mrs. Markland. (hands portemonnaie.)

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Her portemonnaie—how comes this in your hands ?

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: She left it in our office this morning.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: My sister in your office ?

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: Oh, under excellent escort—Mrs. Vernon's. We've a great many ladies among our clients, you know. Meiklam appears at door, L. 2 E. Ah, here's Meiklam at last; now to put on a leetle gentle pressure. (exit, taking Meiklam with him, L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: My sister in the city—I had heard of Mrs. Vernon speculating, but Florry—

div.stage: Enter Markland, Mrs. Vernon and Mrs. Markland, R. C.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Oh, here is Belle to the minute—everybody knows what a woman of business she is. I should enjoy staying with you so much, but I've a hundred things to do, so I must run away, (to Markland) now I've rendered up your treasure; and while you put me in the carriage you shall give me five minutes advice about our investments. Au revoir, sweetest! (to Mrs. Markland) You've been the greatest darling! Good bye, you dear. (to Miss Hargreave. Exeunt Markland and Mrs. Vernon, R. C.)

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: How I hate honey-varnish! (they sit—Mrs. Markland, R. of table, Miss Hargreave, L.) What have you been doing all the morning ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Shopping.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Nothing else ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (after a pause) Nothing particular.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: You must have been inconvenienced by the want of your purse.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: My purse!

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: (giving it) Yes, Mr. Laxton asked me to give it you—it seems you left it in his office this morning.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Hush—not a word of my having been there to my husband. Oh, Belle, I implore you.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I thought you had no secrets.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I have one now, a terrible one.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Florry, you frighten me. You have not been led into speculation by Mrs. Vernon ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: No ! no!

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Then why this anxiety to conceal your visit to Laxton and Fermor's from your husband ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: It is because any question about that might lead to more questioning—questioning I cannot face.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Florry! you have said too much not to speak out now. Was it anything fatal to your happiness as a wife?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, no, he loves me as well as ever.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Nor to his honour as a man ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: No, thank heaven!

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: These safe, what can there be so terrible ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: What I must not reveal, and yet if I am condemned to keep it to myself!—I have not the strength to wear that iron mask !

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Florry, we were one in infancy: we have shared all the joys and sorrows of childhood, must we be less near to each other now we are women. Can you not trust me ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh what a blessed relief it would be to open my heart to you!

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: All the comfort that a sister's love and counsel can give, I would give you. But why not first seek your husband's ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I dare not—my secret is—(they rise and come down) the knowledge that ruin hangs over him by a hair.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Ruin—merciful heaven! Ruin, over him that seemed so prosperous !

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: A debt of £40,000 to Laxton and Fermor must be paid to-day—it is impossible to raise the money.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: But is there no means, no resource ? Men in their position have so many.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I have one hope, my own fortune, but I must have my trustees' consent. Hush !

div.stage: Enter Markland, R. C., down C.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Welcome, both, on your first visit to the bank parlour—its rather dingy.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p:
I call it a delightful old room! (sniffs) With such a venerable perfume about it. A compound, I should
think, of Mr. Meiklam's odour of sanctity and stale money.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I hope you enjoyed your drive.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, (with an effort)—it was very pleasant.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: But you are looking pale ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I'm a little tired, dear—shopping always gives me a headache.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Take care, remember you have a great deal before you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, I know I have.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: The dinner first, and the fête afterwards ; we must all be very gay to-night, if we never mean to be gay again.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: You look fagged and worn, too.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes, it's my first day in harness. There has been a heavy arrear to make up.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: How I wish I could help you. But I suppose a banker's wife mustn't know anything about bank affairs.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Better she should not. How long would home be home if the secrets of the prison house were brought into it ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I thought we had agreed to have no secrets?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: None of our own, but you forget bank secrets are my partner's as well as mine.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: And these grim old gentlemen look as if whole generations of money-mysteries were locked up under their waistcoats. Oh, if these walls could speak !

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: They have ears, but no tongues, happily.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: But we didn't come to pry into the horrors of the bank parlour—we've a secret of our own, you know, Harry.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes, and you want my judgment—I'm at your service.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Mayn't I come ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Oh, dear no; she's to be kept quite in the dark, isn't she Harry ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes, stay here till we return, darling : you won't be dull?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, no, I shall manage to amuse myself— but don't be long, Harry.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Shall I stay with you, and leave Belle to manage her surprise alone ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: No, no, I shall be all the better for a few minutes to myself. Go, dear, (he kisses her and takes her hand. She looks wistfully in his face—he turns away suddenly.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Come, Belle.

div.stage: Exeunt Markland and Miss Hargreave, R. C.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (bursts into tears) I could not have held out a moment longer. He will not trust me—oh, why will he not? It would be a joy even to divide the load of his suffering. But oh, if I could avert it by help of my own fortune—now is my chance to speak with Meiklam.

div.stage: Enter Meiklam, followed by Locksmith L. 2 E., and Laxton.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: The moment I can remedy this unaccountable accident to the strong room door you may rely on having your cheque.

sp.speaker: Laxton.
sp.p: Thank you; delay is death to us, and it would not look well for you. (exit L. 3 E.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Now, my man, (to Locksmith) that's the lock, and here's the key. Ah, Mrs. Markland, this is indeed an honour to our dingy parlour, (goes up to Locksmith.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (salutes him coldly, aside) How my heart recoils from this man, yet I must confide in him.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (to Locksmith, who has opened door with key) What! the lock all right? Very extraordinary! It wouldn't go in just now. Ah, that'll do! (exit Locksmith, L. 2 E. (to Mrs. Markland) To what good fortune do we owe this visit ? and where is Markland ? (brings down Harrington's deed box from safe and puts it on table.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (seated L. of table C.) He has just gone with my sister on a little scheme of their own. Mr. Meiklam, are we safe from interruption here ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Perfectly.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I may trust your discretion ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Implicitly, (sits R. of C. table.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: You are one of the trustees under my marriage settlement ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Yes, with an excellent colleague, Mr. Molesworth. You are well protected.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: What is the amount of my fortune ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: About fifty thousand pounds, more or less.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I want that money put at my husband's disposal.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Mrs. Markland!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I know that the firm is in difficulties—don't ask me how—that to meet these requires the immediate command of a large sum—I wish that sum advanced out of my fortune.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Out of your fortune ! Are you aware, my dear madam, what the law would call us if we consented to do this?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: What ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Fraudulent trustees, madam. Why we should be personally responsible for every penny of the money.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, but my consent surely would bear you harmless. What business can a wife have with a fortune when her husband has debts requiring to be paid ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Bless your innocent heart! Pay his debts out of your private fortune ! there never was such a thing heard of.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Then it's time there should be. Oh, Mr. Meiklam, you have much to answer for in all this.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Me, my dear madam! Nay, I cannot allow

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: No matter, I do not want to reproach you, I only want you to do this for me, and use your influence to get the consent of Mr. Molesworth.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: My dear child, I admire your fine sense of probity, it is quite consonant to my own feelings. But Mr. Molesworth cannot be expected to take the same high view of the matter as you and I.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (rises) Then I will appeal to him.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Take care, my dear madam, or you might really bring on the firm the ruin you are now imagining. No, no,—this is a temporary difficulty—quite an everyday affair in tight times. Next birthday, we will laugh over your fears together.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, my husband does not think so.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Good heavens ! you haven't breathed a syllable of your fears to him ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: No, but I have read his face.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (aside) Ah, I always say married men ought to lock up their looks like a private ledger.

div.stage: Re-enter Markland and Miss Hargreave R. C.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: (who has a jewel case in her hand) Mystery of mysteries ! Now, Fatima, what would you give for a peep ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I've no curiosity, have I ? (to Markland) and if I had—

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Let us hope there is no blue chamber to tempt it. Is your headache better ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Yes, I'm quite well now.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Sure ? Let me look at you. (takes her aside) Have you succeeded ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (aside to her) No.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Well, Belle, your report ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Not encouraging.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You must get home, darling, in time to lie down before dinner; you'll need all your strength and spirits for to-night—I'll put you in the carriage.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Won't you come home with us ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: If you'll wait a few minutes: I've still some business to settle.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I can't wait, I've no end of shopping still to do, so I'll be independent of you both and take a cab. (aside to Mrs. Markland) Don't despair yet. (exit R. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (to herself) Perhaps he will tell me when we are alone. (Markland comes down and takes his wife out R. C.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Time presses—we must have the money. If Laxton and Fermor go, we go with them, (rises.)

div.stage: Re-enter Markland R. C.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Happy fellow, what a wife!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And what a fate you have made for her !

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Again this sinful despondency! I've inquired the market price of these securities—they're A 1.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (R.) Do you hear me, Meiklam ? I have been your unconscious tool till now; I may be destined to become your victim ; but, at last, I have resumed authority here, and I mean to assert it. You shall not touch these securities ! (laying his hand on the box.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Will you tell me another way to raise the money ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I know of none ; but I would not soil my conscience with this breach of trust.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Then you prefer a stoppage ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: A thousand times.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: With the consequences of exposure ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Promise me at least not to resort to these securities—till all other means have been tried.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Willingly, but if the worst comes to the worst—

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: The round of wrong—crime to avert dishonour !

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: I will take the responsibility—I have sources of strength you know nothing of.

div.stage: Enter Scratchell, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: Mrs. Markland is waiting.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I will join her. (exit Scratchell, L. 2 E. As he passes, his eye falls on his father's portrait) Father! (turns away) No, I can never face those eyes again, (exit, R.C.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: (looking at his watch) Half-past three—the money must be found by four—all other means have been tried—there is such a thing as pushing delicacy too far. (opens box and takes securities—Frank appears at door, R. C., watching) But I won't leave Markland in the dark, (writes) It is my duty to let him know what I've done—now it is too late to prevent it. (rings bell.)

div.stage: Enter Scratchell, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Scratchell, ask the messenger to call me a Hansom, and let Mr. Markland has this note to-night.

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: I'll take it to Putney myself—Mrs. Markland has been kind enough to invite me to the fête. (exit, L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p:
(relocking box) Safe bind, but not safe find
exactly—we can replace them at the next turn of the market! Now for it, I shall be just in time, (going, L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (putting his head in at door, R. C.) Nailed ! (Act drop quick.)

div.stage: SCENE. —The stage represents an elegant drawing, room in the Rosery, decorated in white and gold, and brilliantly lighted. The centre compartment communicates by folding-doors with Markland's study. The compartments on either side are arched, and communicate with side-rooms or corridors, also brilliantly lighted and decorated with exotics and statuary. These openings are practicable, and admit of the passage of dancers: flower-stands in the angles, ottomans and light chairs. Music: as the curtain rises, the stage is occupied by a dance, and the movement of a crowded and brilliant fête is seen at its height. As the dance ceases, the couples, who have taken part in it, disperse through the different openings; among these couples are Frank Meiklam and his partner, Markland and Miss Vernon, Mrs. Vernon and Fermor, Harrington and Mrs. Markland, Laxton and Miss Hargreaves. Markland resigns Miss Vernon to her mother, and moves among the company, exchanging salutations, &c. Company disperses.
Enter Mr. Harrington and Miss Hargreaves, L. arch.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Yonder goes Florry.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Oh, she's very well engaged, depend on it.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: She exerts herself so to make everyone happy ; she has quite a gift that way. (sighs)

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Ah, some people can make others happy, without exerting themselves; at least I know one who can.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Who ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: You ! You've made me supremely happy, without in the least exerting yourself.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Oh, but galloping is a very great exertion, and I'm dreadfully tired.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Pray sit down, (they sit, L. c.) I don't mean by galloping, but by simply being what you are. It depends on you, Miss Hargreave, whether——

div.stage: Enter Frank Meiklam, R.U. E.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Ah, Miss Hargreave, I've been looking for you everywhere. Will you give me the pleasure of this deux temps ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I am engaged.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: No. 5 then ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I am engaged for the next eight, and I must see if I survive them before I engage myself deeper.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: At least let me take the chance of survivorship for the ninth, (aside) Hang that fellow, there's no getting a word with her for him. (to Harrington) By the way, Mrs. Markland's looking for you.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: I'll send her to you.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (drily) Pray don't trouble yourself.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Not the least trouble, (aside) I'll put a spoke in his wheel at all events, the insolent beggar.

div.stage: (exit, R. U. E.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I'm quite rested now. (rises, and going)

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: For pity's sake, give me a moment. Miss Hargreave. I was saying, when that fellow interrupted us, that it depends on you, whether we were to call each other partners, not for the next waltz or galop, but for life!

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Mr, Harrington ! that question is too serious to be asked or answered in a ball-room!

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: When may I ask it ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: When you are calmer, and I less disposed to prize my own freedom, and to think sadly of married life.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: You think sadly of married life, with your sister's happiness always before you.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: May not even happiness have its lessons ? And what does it teach so much as distrust of what we are, still more of what we seem to others. Besides, I am very independent; I like to be mistress of my own acts, my own money.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Pray don't let that horrid word be mentioned between us.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: And yet, as the world goes, what is there on which the happiness of marriage depends more ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: I don't want to go as the world goes. I think women should know nothing about money, except how to spend it.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: So you told me this morning, and I hoped your wife wouldn't hold the same theory. Were I your wife, we should not agree upon that point.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Then, let us drop the subject. The next thing will be to claim for women the right, not merely to talk about money, but to manage it.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Their own, I think, they ought; and I think if we had more power of the purse many households would be happier for it!

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Of course a woman's fortune should be settled on herself.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: That would not satisfy me.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: What more could you want ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: The right to dispose of it absolutely.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: No married woman ever has that. Miss Hargreave, it startles me to hear you talk so.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I see it does, and I'm sorry for it.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: If there is one thing that seems to me unnatural in a woman it is this anxiety for independence, and in money matters above all.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I should grieve to lose your good opinion—I feel I must make a large demand on my husband's confidence.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: At least let it come after marriage. But this kind of preliminary stipulation has an odious air of mistrust.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Mistrust! (rises) Not on my part.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p:
I hoped that matters had reached that point
when my opinion would weigh with you. I fear I have been too hasty.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: If you think so, there is no step taken that cannot be retraced, (music—waltz.)

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: You need not remind me of that, (aside) Is she trying me—or is she really as calculating as she seems ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I see my partner for number three in search of me. (Laxton appears from R. arch, she goes towards him, takes his arm, they go off.)

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Have I been blind all this time, or am I dreaming now ? Is this cold bargainer for her rights the girl I have loved so truly !

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Vernon, R. U. E.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Harrington, Cecilia is sighing for her partner—poor dear, she is so impulsive—what a contrast to Miss Hargreave ! Now that is a woman of business in the best sense of the word.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Is there a good sense of the word as applied to women ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: What ? You don't think so ? Entre nous, no more do I—but I thought in your relations with Miss Hargreave I mustn't breathe anything of the kind.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: There is nothing in my relations with Miss Hargreave to require you to modify your opinions, Mrs. Vernon.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Ah, how misinformed I've been—I thought it was all settled—but as it isn't I can only say I'm glad of it. A character such as your's would never have done with a cold, calculating, ambitious nature like hers. An old woman may be excused for saying that you are a prize worth any girl's ambition, especially a girl who has a keen eye for money.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Mrs. Vernon, though I have no right to defend Miss Hargreave, still such an imputation—

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p:
Oh dear, no imputation whatever—but one must draw one's inferences you know. Shall we look for Cecilia ? Ah, there is a child of nature—I can hardly trust her to spend even her own allowance; such a dear,
generous, simple girl; you would like her I'm sure if you knew her—but she's so retiring. (exeunt, L.U. E.)

div.stage: Enter Miss Hargreave and Frank Meiklam, R. u. E.
It is evident they are both excited—he piqued.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Mr. Meiklam, I have only to repeat what I have said already—I will not listen to another word on the subject.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Two negatives are equivalent to an affirmative, you know—you've said "no" twice, mayn't I construe it into "yes ? "

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: This becomes very like a persecution, sir.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Forgive me, it is my love makes me so urgent —I tell you again, I have—at least, I shall have—your sister's and brother's sanction.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: And even if you had their sanction, sir—but you must excuse me if I still think this impossible.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Will you believe it if you hear it from their own mouths—then stay here till I can bring them to you. (exit, R.U. E.)

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: This assurance is intolerable; I only disliked him till to-night, now I hate him. There's George with Mrs. Vernon, I shall fare hardly between them, I'm afraid, now—there was a time when he would have defended me against the claws she carries under her velvet.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Markland, R.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: So sad, Belle—and yet Harrington has just left you ? Ah, this is what I feared—the shadow of my secret is upon you already.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: And not even his attentions can lighten it. (Miss Hargreave turns away to conceal her distress) Is it not terrible to have any concealment from those you love ? Now you know what I have been suffering.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Yes, I think I do, and worse perhaps.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, I pray not.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Florry, in future you must not couple Harrington's name with mine as you did just now.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: What do you mean? He loves you, you know he loves you, he has told me so.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Not now—he has found that we do not understand each other on a very serious subject—money. He thinks me mercenary—let him think so, I will not stoop to justify myself—I see him coming this way, I cannot meet him. (exit, R.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But I must! Think her mercenary! The man who thinks that must answer his belief to me. How miserable he looks. Oh, is my happiness to be like the poison tree—blighting all that comes under its shadow !

div.stage: Enter Harrington, L.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (aside) Her sister—I can trust her. (to Mrs. Markland) I have much to say to you—it concerns your siser's happiness as well as my own.

div.stage: Markland appears with Guests, R.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Here comes my husband—let us stand up in this quadrille, we can talk then without being noticed. (exeunt L., taking Harrington's arm—as they go off, Markland comes down, R., meeting Frank, who comes down L.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: A most successful ball; I've been at a great many brilliant things this season and I've seen nothing in better style—lots of flowers, plenty of light, and no end of pretty women.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Three of the four wheels a ball should run on, the fourth being plenty of white soup, very hot, and champagne, very cold—you'll find both in the supper-room.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Thank you, I'm a dancing man.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yonder are the dancing-rooms, don't let me detain you.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: You're very kind, but I wanted a few minutes conversation. Mr. Markland, you know all about me—

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (drily) Yes!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p:
I'm not conceited, but I know I've a head on my shoulders—I've long admired Miss Hargreave, and
as I like doing things above board, I wish to ask your sanction of my addresses as her natural guardian.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I've heard you out, sir, by some effort of patience. But I find considerable difficulty in giving you an answer.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Oh, take your time about it.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I'm afraid the more time I take about it, the more difficult the task will be. Are you aware, when you venture to make this proposal, that you only hold your place in the bank on sufferance—that had you been called to account as strictly as other clerks would have been, your irregularities might have had more serious consequences even than dismissal ? Yet you, who I am astonished to see here, even as a guest—

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Here's your wife's invitation—(shows note)— "particularly requests"—the "particularly" underlined you see!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You dare ask me to sanction your addresses to my sister-in-law ? I won't say "leave my house," but I should think you would hardly like to stay in it after what I have said to you.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: But you haven't answered my question. Will you sanction my addresses to Miss Hargreave—in two words?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: In one word. No !

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Ah, I'm sorry for that; I'm quite aware the lady is her own mistress, but I understand she has determined not to marry without your approval, I don't intend to leave this house till I have it.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: If your only objection is one of character, I don't think that ought to stand in the way between you and me.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: What do you mean by this insolence ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: That if I have been looseish, you have been dishonest—that if I'm a bit of a rip, it rests with me to prove you a thief.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: A thief!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Yes, keeping fraudulent books may be simple roguery, but appropriating securities is decidedly thieving, and punishable by statute with transportation.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (alarmed) Hush, hush ! this is not a place—

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: So I should have thought. But you began the game of disagreeable truths, and I'm only following suit. I heard every word that passed in the bankparlour, this afternoon, between you and my venerable relative. I have but to speak to consign you to the infamy of the felon's dock—the felon's sentence—the felon's jacket.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And the price of your silence ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Is merely your sanction of my addresses to your sister-in-law, including, of course, the discountenancing of all rivals.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And do you think I will consent to this infamous bargain ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: I think its about the best thing you can do. I'm very fond of her. I don't mind if half her fortune's settled on herself.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: This is intolerable!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Not so bad as the Old Bailey dock, and Pentonville to follow.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: At least you will leave me some time for reflection.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Oh, any time in reason; bat I should like an answer to-night. (exit, L.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Miserable man that I am; his evidence would be my doom. But what proof is there that Meiklam has already appropriated these securities? He promised only to resort to them, when all else failed. He may have found other resources. No, I will not believe it, without better proof than this villain's assertion.

div.stage: Enter Scratchell, L.U. E.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Well, Scratchell, I hope you are amused.

sp.speaker: Scratch.
sp.p: A most magnificent entertainment, Mr. Markland, magnificent! Quite dazzling—in fact, it has dazzled me. I ought to have given you this note of Mr. Meiklam's when I arrived, but really what with the rooms, and the lights, and the flowers, and the ladies—I've got a partner waiting for me now.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p:
Don't disappoint her, pray. (Scratchell retires,
c. Opening note and reading) " My dear young friend,"— his friend!—" Before you receive this, H's securities will be in the broker's hands. I really could not allow your scruples to imperil the existence of the firm at such a critical moment. Your affectionate old friend and partner, Ephraim Meiklam." No hope—no doubt the deed is done—I am a dishonoured man!

div.stage: Mrs. Markland comes down from L. U.E.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Harry, I am so grieved; there has been a serious misunderstanding between Belle and Harrington.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Indeed—what about ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: The root of all mischief—money. He has proposed to her.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Proposed to Belle! (aside) With my disgrace hanging over her head, poor girl—and this threat of Meiklam's!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: You don't disapprove, I hope ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: No, he is everything I could wish her husband, but just now there are reasons why I should wish him not to press his offer.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I saw Mr. Frank Meiklam with you just now. Has he anything to do with this hesitation—I know he is himself an admirer of Belle's.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: He has asked me to sanction his addresses to her.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: You have refused, of course ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: No, not refused, exactly.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But not sanctioned, surely ? Oh, Harry, consider—a man with his manners, habits, and character —

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You cannot think worse of him than I do, but I can't quarrel with him at this moment; in fact, Florry, he is in possession of a secret which I dare not reveal even to you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Suppose I know this terrible secret already?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Heaven forbid!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Do not say so. You do not know how strong I am—how much love can bear—how much love can comfort.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Do not keep me on the rack! Speak out. What do you know ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I was in your broker's office by accident this morning—the difficulties of the firm; it was terrible to know and not speak—but I felt it was for you to decide whether I might be trusted with such a secret.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: (aside, and turning up) Thank heaven she knows of nothing worse than ruin.

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Vernon, two Ladies, and Miss Hargreave, L.

sp.speaker: Mrs. V.
sp.p: Mr. Markland, will you come and play showman to your beautiful pictures ? We are a set of perfect ignoramuses, and beg to be enlightened.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: That way, ladies; I am at your service, (goes up and off with then, L.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: (beckons Miss Hargreave from the group, and comes down with her) Belle, I have seen Harrington, he is wretched—I have promised him an explanation from you—you owe it to his deep affection for you to remove this impression.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: It is for him to own that he has misjudged me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: There is obstinacy in the pride that will not condescend to its own justification. For a miserable question of money would you risk the happiness of your life?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: What if the happiness of two lives should hang on this miserable question.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Belle, you amaze me, this persistence is unworthy of you—unbecoming—almost unwomanly.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: One cannot alter one's nature at one-and twenty.

div.stage: Enter Harrington, L.—Mrs. Markland goes up.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Miss Hargreave, your sister insists upon it that I have misunderstood you—that an explanation —

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I am ready to hear it.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Pardon me I have nothing to explain.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Nor have I.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: I am sorry for it; I thought you had felt on reflection that the moment I was offering you my heart was ill-chosen for stipulations about money.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: I knew your prejudice against women who think of such things.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Because when they do, in my eyes, they cease to be women. (Mrs. Markland comes forward, c.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: This is folly—Belle and you are playing with each other's hearts like children, at the risk of breaking them; I will not allow it. I know, Mr. Harrington, so far from being interested ——

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Florry, I am here to speak and act for myself ; Mr. Harrington has not misunderstood my anxiety to keep my fortune under my own control——

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: (to Mrs. Markland) And I was wrong to call her distrustful.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: But it is right he should know why I did so, because I had already found employment for my money—

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: An admirable woman of business!

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Which I could not alter, and which I knew trustees under a marriage settlement would not approve.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: No doubt they object to speculative investments.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But, Belle, these are not considerations for such a moment.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: You must allow me to be the best judge of that.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: You hear ! (goes up, L. c.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Be warned in time, he is deeply wounded— for pity's sake do not trifle thus with his feelings.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Trifle!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I cannot believe that you would seriously sacrifice his affection to your fortune.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Harrington may misjudge me, but I should be safe from your reproaches, Florry. (goes up.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Can she be indeed the selfish calculator, Harrington thinks? Oh, no! I cannot have been so mistaken in a sister. Enter Markland, L. Harry, do you help me to bend her stubborn will.

div.stage: Frank appears watching, L. U. E.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p:
What, still sulking ? As if life had not solid
miseries enough, that we should create phantom ones— come, Harrington, Belle, this must not be. (they come in on in answer to his appeal.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (coming down, L.) The very conjunction I was trying to bring about. (Harrington is about to retire with Miss Hargreave) Pray stay, you are anything but de trop. (to Markland) Will you satisfy Miss Hargreave I was not speaking without book when I said I had your sanction for my addresses to her.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: His sanction ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I refuse it.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Don't be too hasty, (to Markland) Third parties present too. Hadn't you better re-consider your answer—I think you must have forgotten.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I have forgotten nothing: let them hear, I am sick of concealment: I have weighed the alternative—my misery against hers—I accept my own—and not only do I refuse my sanction, but I warn her——

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: (interrupting) Stay, let me do the warning, (to Mrs. Markland) I warn you against your husband, (to Miss Hargreave) I warn you against your brother-in-law, as a breaker of his trust, a swindler, and a thief.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Liar ! (Markland sinks in chair, R. c, and hides his face.)

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Look at him!

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Coward! You shall answer this to me.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: When and where and as you please—(significantly) after I have given my evidence. You should thank me for bringing him to book—it is your securities they have appropriated, he and my worthy uncle together. (to the Ladies) But I ought to ask your pardon, such charges should be brought and proved elsewhere; I will save my proofs for the witness-box of the Old Bailey.

div.stage: (exit, L.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Florry, what does this mean ? your husband does not speak. Is it all a horrible dream ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p:
(sees Guests enter, R. and L.) Hush, command yourself as I do. Mr. Harrington, not a word of this for mercy's sake. It is not true, of course—all can be explained, but this is no time—help me to conceal his
agitation from these people—make them begin the next dance at once, (all the Guests are now well on) Ah, Mr. Harrington, Belle has kept the next waltz open for you. (Harrington takes Miss Hargreave up, Mrs. Markland occupies the attention of the Guests with forced gaiety) Miss Vernon, here is Mr. Laxton longing for a deux temps; Mr. Scratchell, let me introduce you to a partner, I won't have you standing out. Mr. Fermor, you are bound to set an example to your juniors, (finding him a partner.)

sp.speaker: Fermor.
sp.p: (to Scratchell) What a happy, bright creature it is!

div.stage: (Guests go off R. and L., with new partners.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Now we are alone. Husband, you heard what that man said ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I heard.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: You did not give the lie to his atrocious words ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I shall have to bear their weight before the world.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: What do you mean ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: In the eyes of the world and of the law, I shall be held all he called me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Oh, no, no !

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I have been the tool of a villain. I must take the consequences. Yes, Florry, Markland, the fraudulent banker, the appropriator of his client's securities, will be the nine days wonder of the police reports, the mark of the finger of public scorn, the butt for the cruel pity, or contemptuous cynicism, for the very guests that crowd these rooms. Oh, where shall I find strength to face all this?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: In the calm of your own conscience, in the faithfulness of my love.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Can you answer even for that ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Aye, if you can look me in the face, and with your hand in mine, thus, (taking his hand) say, "Wife, by the love between us, I am innocent."

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: And if I refused the test ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: But you will not, I know you will not.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p:
The wife who is to stand alone against the
world's judgment must seek strength to do so in her love alone, love that dispenses with assurance, asks not for proof, stays not to balance assertions or weigh probabilites, but says, "There is my husband, my place is at his side, in the dock, in the cell, aye, if need be, on the scaffold." Ask yourself, Florry, if your love be of that temper, and if it be—perhaps—for ever then, I know not—I may find in it a support against despair, (exit, c.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: He will not give me the assurance I ask. He appeals to my love, my love alone, as if he could seek in that the stay his own conscience cannot give him. Can it be that he has trusted Meiklam so far that the step from embarrassment to crime became inevitable ? Let me face the worst—were it even so, could I, in the face of the world's scorn, take his hand and say, "I will cling the closer, because all turn from you: now that respect and honour, and fair fame are gone, my love shall be to you all in all. Yes, if I know my own heart, I have the strength, and if the awful need come, I will prove it. Husband, dearest, I ask no test, I impose no condition—innocent or guilty, I am still your own. (goes to door c, and knocks gently) Harry, let me in, please—it is Florry, your own Florry. (knocks louder) I have asked myself that question, I bring you the answer. One word—one word, for pity's sake, speak to me. Still silent ? I can bear this no longer. (opens the door and fnds the room empty) Gone, the window open—what does this mean ? Ah ! the river ! (screams and falls senseless—Guests waltz on.)

div.stage: Act drop.

SCENE.—The River Terrace—moonlight—R, a balustrade terrace in the grounds, with steps leading to the Thames. In flat, the river, with the lights of the far off bridges, &c, twinkling in the distance, and nearer the house lighted
up. On the R. shrubs and trees coming down upon the stage which is covered with green sward, except near the terrace, which has a pavement of encaustic tiles—stone seats along the terrace.
Markland discovered seated, l. c.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Alone at last—face to face with my shame! Till to-day, honourable and happy—to-night so miserable —to-morrow, oh, what will to-morrow bring with it— detection, exposure, infamy—and my wife—ah, there is the intolerable burden, to blight this young life, which I have linked to my own, when I should have blessed it. To crush the trustful heart I have cherished till every pang I feel will strike through it like a knife, (clock strikes twelve) Midnight! so ends the day that dawned so brightly ! Oh, what a morrow is opening for me, for her! Coward that I am to parley thus with my wretchedness, when a moment's resolution might end it. How calm the river looks in the moonlight—its dark, deep waters roll smoothly on, betraying no chafe of sand or shoal, burying all foulness under them, sweeping all waifs and strays alike to the unfathomable sea.
sp.stage: Enter Mrs. Markland, L. U. E., watching him.
sp.p: Why should it not bury my shame with its other pollutions, and bear me down, a wreck of the great city, to the merciful waters of forgetfulness ? (as he approaches the steps, Mrs. Markland, by a great effort, masters a scream and rapid movement towards him) My death would cause her less misery than my life. Yes, my darling, there is love even in the act that separates us for ever.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Harry dear!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Too late! (he turns) Ah, Florry !

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I discovered you had played truant—I'm so glad I've found you: you must not stay here by the river: the damps are dangerous : besides, you will be missed in the house. Come back with me.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Back to the mirth and music yonder ? Florry, I cannot. The darkness and silence of the night cool my brain! Go you back and leave me here.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Is my place among that mirth and music when you are in suffering and sorrow ?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Never mind me; your absence will be observed —go, it is my wish.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: No, please.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Go, Florry, it is my order.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Dearest, you have not been used to speak so to me. You are unhappy—my place is near you; you dread the world's reproach, you must not doubt my sympathy; you fear the desertion of your friends, then double, triple, tenfold need of the presence of your wife.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Heaven bless you for this comfort!

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: You laid a burden on me when you left me: you bade me prove myself if I had strength to bear it— dearest, I have strength; I ask no question about your temptation or your fall—I only know that you are unhappy, and that I love you more, if that be possible, than I did before this cloud darkened our lives; there is only one thing I cannot bear, that you should not be strong enough to face the consequences of your act, be they what they may. Despair is cowardly. I could not bear to think my Harry a coward; despair is doubt of Heaven's mercy, and we know how great and free that is despair shuts the door on repentance and makes reparation impossible, and our work henceforth must be to repent and to atone.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Oh, what is men's boasted strength to the calm courage of a loving woman. Florry, you make a man of me again. I will not crown the weakness of my sin by the baser weakness, that to escape man's justice flies in the face of Heaven.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: That's like your own dear self—let the world frown in condemnation or scorn, you can turn from it to my face, and there you shall never read anything but love.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Heaven forgive my desperate thoughts! I will expiate my sin by endurance now, in hopes the day may come when I shall expiate it by reparation.

div.stage: Enter Frank Meiklam and Miss Hargreave, L.U.E.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Belle with him!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: I guessed you had gone out to think over the situation—I have been thinking it over too : I have been too hasty.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I thought you could not be quite without mercy.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: You only did me justice. Mr. Markland, all that passed at the bank to-day remains a secret between us.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Is it possible ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I dare scarce believe it, but if this be true, oh, how I will pray for you, and bless you.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: A bride in hand is worth two blessings in the bush ! Don't thank me, thank your sister, Mrs. Frank Meiklam that is to be.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Belle!

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You have consented to become his wife ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Why what do you suppose I had changed my mind for ? Yes, we have agreed to make each other happy, I ask no settlements, nor does she—there's only one condition, I'm to have a junior partnership.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: If you join the firm, I leave it. (to Miss Harrington) I appreciate your generosity, but you shall not forfeit your life's happiness for me.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Who talks of forfeiting happiness ? I have accepted Mr. Meiklam of my own free will.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Belle, this is mistaken self-devotion—for us, the bitterness of this hour over, we can face the worst together—but to know that your happiness, as well as my husband's good name were in his power

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: He commits himself by joining the firm.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: To buy his silence by your misery.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Misery, why we have so many tastes in common——

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Belle, you amaze me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Can it be my sister who talks thus ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Besides, he leaves me mistress of my fortune.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Unrestrictedly, (aside) But no settlements.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Still thinking of money ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: That's what I like in her, she's a thorough woman of business.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You promised not to marry without my sanction —I refuse it.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: It was an inconsiderate promise, and does not bind me in reason or in law.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Belle, for the love that was once between us——

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: It is too late, I have made up my mind.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Hey, hallo! Mr. Markland! (enters breathless, l.U. E.) Ah, Mr. Markland, enjoying the delights of an al fresco ? I should apologize for this rather abrupt intrusion on your fête—in the first place, without a card, in the second place, without a tail-coat; but I hope——

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Your business here, Mr. Rocket ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: That's the tone I like: prompt, and to the point! I come as herald, harbinger, feathered Mercury, agent in advance—whatever you like that goes express pace, and brings good news

sp.speaker: Molesworth.
sp.p: Rocket, hey! where are you ? Do you want to break my neck ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: There's Mr. Molesworth—not quite so fast as the Rocket. I'll throw a light on the situation. The man who meets me will always meet with his match. (strikes match) My new patent poluphloisboio-magnesium light, or every man his own moonshine, (holding up match) Signal hoisted, all right, line clear, move ahead gently, avoiding the ditches !

div.stage: Enter Molesworth and Meiklam followed by Harrington, L. U. E.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: At last! (Meiklam bows to Mr. and Mrs. Markland and sits on garden seat, l.) Markland, my dear Mrs. Markland, I wish you all many, many happy returns of the day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: You wished me that this morning, (aside, and with a sigh) Too soon !

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: But not with half such reason, (gives Markland a paper) Here are Harrington's securities. Luckily I had a duplicate key of the box—found it empty— started in chase, and, thanks principally to Mr. Rocket here, rescued them just on the broker's threshold.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Beaten on all my line.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: At least I shall be spared the infamy of a criminal charge! But ruin is still imminent.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Yes, this very hasty act of Mr. Molesworth's will bring down Laxton and Fermor by the run, and we shall be involved in the crash.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: No, I must tell you now. They hold my note of hand for your debt. (Frank whistles)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yours! How did you know ?

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: I told her. Then when you left us at the Bank——

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: The transfer department was closed, so I gave my note of hand and the Stock is to be transferred to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Stop, stop, Miss Hargreave, we did agree there were to be no settlements, but it seems you had nothing substantial to settle.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: And you nothing substantial to disclose. There has been a failure of consideration on both sides. As a woman of business, I fancy that annuls the contract.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Her fortune first and herself afterwards. And this is the heart we dared suspect. Bless you, Belle. But why did you not tell me what you contemplated ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Because I knew that neither he nor you would have consented to what you were sure to call a sacrifice, but what I, as a woman of business, knew was a capital investment. I shall get five per cent, for my money, they only give me three and a half in the funds, you know.

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: And you can forgive my hastiness, my distrust ?

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: If you can forgive my knowing at least this much about money, that it is never so well ventured as in aid of those we love.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: But this is too desperate a venture. I cannot avail myself of it.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p:
My dear sir, you are not so elastic as your own resources. To-night's mail has brought a large
remittance on account of Wildman and Waters, and prospect of more.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Then there is still hope; but what further confidence can there be between me and this man ?

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Ah, if there had been but more confidence ere this!

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I'm afraid the house of Markland and Meiklam must disappear from the banker's list.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: So old established a firm, and so respectable!

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Now that you have consented to withdraw from it.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Yes, I am prepared to sacrifice my prospects.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Including the Old Bailey dock. Of course you will take with you your precious nephew here ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Thank you; I'm perfectly ready to retire from the bank; but I distinctly decline anything like solidarity with my venerable uncle, (turns on his heel.)

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Unhappy boy! Now he is left to himself, what will become of him ?

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: I have written off my debt now, Mr. Meiklam. I'd not have anything to say to you, sir, (with withering contempt) not even as a director!

div.stage: (Mrs. Markland comes forward, with Miss H. and Harrington.)

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: You'll still take my money. Harry, will you not?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Ah, Molesworth, what a lesson in self-sacrifice this noble girl has read us all.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: Sacrifice! Mr. Molesworth knows a great deal better than that.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: I know if I could slip thirty years off my back, and Mrs. Molesworth—

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Hold hard, sir. I think you'd better not go any further. You hear, sir—Belle still presses her offer.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: You do not suppose I can accept it ?

sp.speaker: Harring.
sp.p: Perhaps you'll be kinder to me, though I've two requests to make. First, this dear girl's hand—and then a partnership. I shall be sure to make ducks and drakes of my money, if its left in my own hands.

sp.speaker: Miss H.
sp.p: You forget, sir, you will have me to look after it—there'll be one at least in the firm who will be wide awake.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: With good handling the house will right itself yet. Its not Markland and Meiklam now.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Mr. Molesworth, I'm a worm. I'm aware I'm a worm, and I hope I feel as a worm should; but even the worm will turn, Mr. Molesworth.

sp.speaker: Moles.
sp.p: Turn, by all means—towards the entrance-gate yonder, but don't forget your undertaking goes beyond retirement from the firm. He has bound himself to leave this country.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Yes, thank Heaven, in the new world there is an opening for piety and principle.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: Oh, you're too smart for the Yankees.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: There's Australia.

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: What a comfort to think you'll have to pay your own passage money. But wherever he goes, I wish the land of his adoption joy of him.

sp.speaker: Meik.
sp.p: Some men might call this ruin, but I have faith— and these are the moments when faith sustains one. My faith teaches me to forgive you—yes, I forgive all!

div.stage: (exit, L. 2 E.)

sp.speaker: Rocket.
sp.p: My young friend, don't you think you'd better get up a cab for your venerable uncle ?

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.p: Eh ? ah! no! I don't see it. (going) Good night, Markland. Tata, ladies ; good night!

div.stage: (lights cigar, and exit jauntily, L.U.E.)

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: With Harrington's capital in the business, this contract debt lightened, and dishonour averted, there is hope before me still. Oh, how I will toil to make it good. I know my weakness now ; I will use the knowledge when the tempter suggests the first step, though it be but a hair's breadth, from the straight way of truth and honour.

sp.speaker: Mrs. M.
sp.p: Amen, my dearest; chastened by this suffering, and strong in this resolve, we may look forward— (to Audience) Oh, say we may look forward without fear—even to the award on "Settling Day."

div.stage: CURTAIN.
